title: Introduction to EdgeSwarm
content:
# Introduction to EdgeSwarm

EdgeSwarm is a decentralized edge-AI network where autonomous agents collaborate, execute tasks, and settle payments on Solana with independent verification. In this guide, you will learn exactly how introduction to edgeswarm works inside EdgeSwarm, why it exists, how to use it safely, and how to debug it when something goes wrong. EdgeSwarm is built on a simple promise: agents that work, proof that pays. That promise only holds if every step is verifiable, every payment is policy-checked, and every receipt can be checked by anyone later. This page is written for builders, hackers, reviewers, and judges at the Solana Hackathon who want the full picture, not just a marketing summary. Read it end to end for your first pass, then use it as a reference while you build. By the end, you will be able to explain introduction to edgeswarm to a teammate, implement it in a demo, and defend your design choices in a review.

## Why Introduction to EdgeSwarm Matters

Introduction to EdgeSwarm is not a side feature. It is a load-bearing part of the EdgeSwarm trust story. Without it, you are back to trusting a single server, a single model, or a single human claim. With it, you get a system where a job on a real edge device can be checked by a different agent on a different host, and payment only happens when both policy checks pass and verification says VERIFIED. That is the difference between a chatbot demo and a machine-to-machine economy. For getting started, the stakes are concrete: budgets are real USDC, even if they are tiny in the demo at $0.10 per job. A bug here means overspend, a tampered result getting paid, or a good worker not getting paid. This guide shows you how EdgeSwarm prevents all three. You will see the exact checks, the exact hashes, and the exact user experience that keeps the main wallet safe while the capped agent wallet does the small, bounded work.

## How Introduction to EdgeSwarm Works in EdgeSwarm

At a high level, EdgeSwarm always follows the same flow: a user creates a budgeted task, Policy Check 1 admits it, EdgeAgent executes it on a real device, ProofAgent independently checks it on a different host, Policy Check 2 plus Exact Message Review gates payment, Solana Devnet settles USDC, and a signed receipt is issued. Introduction to EdgeSwarm sits inside that flow at a precise point. In this section we unpack that point. First, the Coordinator creates a TaskEnvelopeV1 that pins the job definition, input hash, policy hash, budget in micro-USDC, expiry, and nonce. That envelope is hashed to a task hash. Any change to the envelope changes the hash. Second, the worker is assigned and executes under resource limits. Third, the worker signs the result with Ed25519 under a domain-separated context that binds job ID, assignment ID, input digest, output digest, nonce, and policy scope. Fourth, the verifier re-derives the result from trusted inputs and compares canonical bytes. Fifth, only VERIFIED pays. WARNING or REJECTED never authorizes payment. That invariant is enforced in code and in policy, not just in documentation.

### The Core Invariant: Only VERIFIED Pays

If you remember one rule from this entire docs site, remember this: only VERIFIED pays. It sounds simple, but it changes everything. It means the Coordinator cannot pay a job that failed verification, even if the worker insists it is correct. It means a tampered result, even if it looks plausible, is rejected and the reservation is released. It means a job that times out, exceeds its budget, or violates policy is not paid, and the reason is logged with a code. For introduction to edgeswarm, this invariant is checked in two places: in the Coordinator state machine, which refuses to transition a non-VERIFIED job to payment, and in Policy Check 2, which re-validates budget, policy version, and verification level before any transaction is built. In your demo, show this invariant explicitly. Create one good job that verifies and pays, and one tampered job that is rejected. Judges remember the rejected job more than the happy path, because it proves you thought about abuse.

## Step-by-Step Guide: Introduction to EdgeSwarm

This is the hands-on part. Follow these steps in order. Each step builds on the previous one. Do not skip the verification steps, even if your job looks correct. In EdgeSwarm, looking correct is not enough. You need proof.

**Step 1 — Define the goal for introduction to edgeswarm.** Write one sentence: what should happen, what should not happen, and how you will know it worked. For example, for job job_001_introduction, the goal is to produce a result that can be re-derived by a verifier with the same inputs. Keep the goal small. A small, verifiable job beats a large, unverifiable one every time.

**Step 2 — Pin your inputs.** Hash your inputs and record the input hash. If your job uses a document, a CSV, an image, or a source URL, pin it. For GossipMarket-style jobs, pin the source snapshot. For data jobs, pin the CSV bytes. The verifier must use the same pinned inputs, not whatever the worker claims it used.

**Step 3 — Set budget and policy.** Set a budget in micro-USDC. In the demo, use $0.10, which is 100000 micro-USDC. Set caps: $0.10 per job, $1.00 per hour. Set policy version and hash. Record the policy hash in the envelope. If you change policy later, the hash changes and old envelopes are invalid.

**Step 4 — Create the TaskEnvelopeV1.** Build the envelope with jobId, inputHash, policyHash, budget, expiry, and nonce. Hash the canonical envelope to get the task hash. This task hash is your job identity. Share it in logs, in the dashboard, and in your receipt.

**Step 5 — Run Policy Check 1.** The Coordinator checks policy before any work. If the job violates budget, allowlist, quota, or expiry, it is rejected before assignment. This saves device time and money. Log the decision with policy version and reason.

**Step 6 — Assign and execute.** The Coordinator assigns a worker. EdgeAgent executes under CPU, memory, time, and battery limits. The worker signs the result. The signature binds job, assignment, digests, nonce, and policy. If the device goes offline, the job can be retried safely because the nonce and assignment make retries idempotent.

**Step 7 — Verify independently.** ProofAgent fetches the same pinned inputs, replays deterministic work, and compares canonical output bytes. It checks schema at E0, signature at E1, replay at E2, and corroboration at E3 when needed. It never trusts worker assertions. It writes a verification verdict with evidence level and rejection code if needed.

**Step 8 — Run Policy Check 2 and Exact Message Review.** After VERIFIED, Policy Check 2 re-validates budget and policy. Then the user sees the exact message to be signed: recipient, amount, memo, and job binding. The main wallet never auto-signs. Only the capped agent wallet signs, and only after human review in the demo flow.

**Step 9 — Settle on Solana.** The Coordinator builds a Solana Devnet USDC transaction, submits it, confirms it, and reconciles the reservation. Fees are about $0.0002 and settle is about 0.9 seconds in the demo. Record the transaction signature.

**Step 10 — Issue and check the receipt.** EdgeProof issues a signed receipt with task hash, result hash, worker DID, verifier DID, policy hash, and tx signature. Verify the receipt offline: check hashes, check signatures, check policy hash. Save the receipt. It is your portable proof.

## Code Example: Introduction to EdgeSwarm

Below is a simplified TypeScript example that shows the shape of introduction to edgeswarm in code. It is not production code, but it shows the exact fields you must get right. Copy it, adapt it to your job type, and test it on Devnet before you demo.

```pseudocode-unvalidated
// Introduction to EdgeSwarm — simplified EdgeSwarm example
const envelope = {
  jobId: "job_001_introduction",
  inputHash: "sha256:…", // hash of pinned inputs
  policyHash: "sha256:…", // hash of policy version
  budgetMicroUsdc: 100000, // $0.10
  expiresAt: Date.now() + 10 * 60 * 1000,
  nonce: crypto.randomUUID(),
};
const taskHash = await hashCanonical(envelope);
// Policy Check 1
const admitted = await policyCheck1(envelope);
if (!admitted) throw new Error("Policy Check 1 rejected");
// Execute on EdgeAgent, sign with Ed25519
const result = await edgeAgent.execute(envelope);
// Verify with ProofAgent — never trust worker claim
const verdict = await proofAgent.verify(envelope, result);
if (verdict.status !== "VERIFIED") throw new Error(verdict.code);
// Policy Check 2 + Exact Message Review
await policyCheck2(envelope, verdict);
const tx = await buildSolanaPayment(envelope, verdict);
console.log("tx", tx.signature);
```pseudocode-unvalidated

Line by line: the envelope pins everything. The task hash is the identity. Policy Check 1 gates work. Execution signs the result. Verification re-derives it. Policy Check 2 gates payment. The transaction is built only after verification. If any step fails, the job stops and the reservation is released. Notice what is missing: there is no step where the main wallet auto-signs, no step where a WARNING job pays, and no step where the Coordinator trusts the worker. Those omissions are the design. When you review code, check for those omissions. If you see a path where payment happens without VERIFIED, that is a bug. Fix it before mainnet.

## Real Example: Introduction to EdgeSwarm in a Demo

Imagine you are demoing introduction to edgeswarm for judges. You open the dashboard and create a job: “Analyze this document locally. Budget: $0.10.” The dashboard shows the envelope, the task hash, and the policy hash. You press Create. Policy Check 1 passes in milliseconds. EdgeAgent on a real Android device picks up the job. It runs under limits, signs the result, and uploads digests. ProofAgent on a different host fetches the same pinned document, replays the analysis, and matches the result. The dashboard flips to VERIFIED (E2). Policy Check 2 passes. You see the exact message: pay $0.10 USDC to worker DID for job job_001_introduction. You approve with the capped agent wallet. Solana Devnet settles in about 0.9 seconds for about $0.0002. The receipt appears with all hashes and the tx signature. Then you show the tampered variant: you flip one byte in the result, the hash mismatches, verification fails with a clear code, and payment is denied. That second demo is the one judges will remember. It proves you built a system, not a slide deck.

## Best Practices for Introduction to EdgeSwarm

**1. Keep jobs small and deterministic.** Small jobs verify faster and replay cleanly. If your job is nondeterministic, declare it. Do not pretend a random model output is deterministic. Use E3 corroboration for nondeterministic work, and label it honestly.

**2. Pin everything.** Pin inputs, models, code version, and policy. If it is not pinned, it cannot be verified. If it cannot be verified, it cannot be paid. Pinning is not bureaucracy. It is the only way the verifier can do its job.

**3. Use integer micro-USDC everywhere.** Never use floats for money. $0.10 is 100000 micro-USDC. Store it as an integer, reserve it atomically, and reconcile it to the on-chain amount. Floats cause rounding bugs that are hard to debug and easy to exploit.

**4. Log decisions with hashes.** Log task hash, result hash, policy hash, verifier DID, and verdict for every job. Logs without hashes are stories. Logs with hashes are evidence. You will need them for audit, for debugging, and for your hackathon demo.

**5. Test the failure path.** Test tampered results, expired jobs, over-budget jobs, offline workers, and failed verifications. The happy path is easy. The failure path is where trust is built. Write a test for each rejection code and show it in your demo.

## Common Pitfalls and Troubleshooting

**Pitfall: Hash mismatch after a tiny edit.** You changed one character in the input and verification failed. That is correct behavior. The hash changed. Re-pin the input, create a new envelope, and re-run. Do not try to patch the old hash.

**Pitfall: Policy Check 1 passes but Check 2 fails.** Policy changed between creation and verification, or budget was already spent by a concurrent job. Check policy version, check reservations, and re-create with fresh policy hash.

**Pitfall: Verifier says WARNING.** WARNING is not VERIFIED. WARNING never pays. Read the warning code, fix the input or the verifier, and re-run. Do not force a WARNING job to pay.

**Pitfall: Payment stuck or not confirmed.** Check the transaction signature on Devnet explorer, check reservation status, and check if the reservation expired. If it expired, the reservation is released and you need a new job. Do not retry the same transaction with a new nonce without checking reconciliation.

**Pitfall: Agent wallet shows $0 balance.** The agent wallet is intentionally small. Fund it with a small amount, like $2.50 USDC in the demo, and check caps. If it is empty, top it up from your main wallet with human approval and exact message review. Never auto-fund from main wallet.

## Security Notes for Introduction to EdgeSwarm

Security for introduction to edgeswarm starts with separation. The main wallet never auto-signs. The agent wallet is capped. The worker and verifier are in separate trust boundaries. Signatures are domain-separated. Nonces and expiry prevent replay. Policy is versioned and hashed. If any of those separations break, stop and fix it. Do not ship a demo where the main wallet signs automatically, even if it is more convenient. Convenience is not worth a drained wallet. For getting started, also think about privacy. Content never leaves the device unless the job requires it. Only hashes are anchored. If your job handles sensitive data, run it locally, pin the source, and verify the digest, not the raw content. Document what leaves the device and what stays. Judges and users will ask. Have an answer ready that matches your code.

## Checklist: Introduction to EdgeSwarm

Before you call introduction to edgeswarm done, check every box. If you cannot check a box, you are not done. [ ] Envelope pins inputs, policy, budget, expiry, nonce. [ ] Task hash is recorded and shown in UI. [ ] Policy Check 1 passed and is logged. [ ] Worker executed under limits and signed result. [ ] ProofAgent verified independently at stated evidence level. [ ] Policy Check 2 passed. [ ] Exact message was reviewed before signing. [ ] Main wallet never auto-signed. [ ] Agent wallet caps enforced. [ ] Payment confirmed and reconciled. [ ] Receipt issued and verified offline. [ ] Tampered variant tested and rejected. [ ] Logs contain hashes, DIDs, and verdict. If you can check all of them, you have a demo you can defend. If you cannot, fix the unchecked box first.

## FAQ: Introduction to EdgeSwarm

**Q: Does introduction to edgeswarm work on mainnet?** A: Horizon 1 is Devnet for the demo. Mainnet is opt-in, capped at 0.01 SOL, with exact message review and human approval. Do not move to mainnet without the checklist in the Deployment guide.

**Q: What if verification is slow?** A: Check if the job is deterministic and small. Large or nondeterministic jobs take longer to replay. Split large jobs, pin smaller inputs, and use E3 corroboration where needed. Measure replay time and show it in your demo.

**Q: Can I use introduction to edgeswarm without Solana?** A: The verification and policy logic works without Solana, but settlement and receipts are designed for Solana. For the hackathon, use Solana Devnet USDC so payment is verifiable on-chain.

**Q: How do I explain introduction to edgeswarm to a non-technical judge in 30 seconds?** A: Say: We create a small, budgeted job, a real device does it, a different agent checks it independently, and we only pay if it verifies. The receipt proves it. Then show the tampered job being rejected. That is the whole story in 30 seconds.

## Next Steps

You have now read the full guide for introduction to edgeswarm. Next, try it. Create a job for job_001_introduction on Devnet, run it, verify it, and check the receipt. Then break it: tamper with one byte and watch it get rejected. That pair of experiences — one success and one rejection — teaches more than any docs page. After that, read the next page in Getting Started: it builds directly on what you learned here. If you are following the Tutorials track, jump to the tutorial that matches this concept and build it end to end. If you are preparing for the Solana Hackathon, use this page as your talking points: explain the invariant, show the hashes, show the receipt, and show the rejection. That is how you win trust, and that is how EdgeSwarm wins. The machine-to-machine economy starts with one verified job. Build yours now.

# Setting Up Your Devnet Wallet

Create a Solana Devnet wallet, fund it with Devnet SOL and USDC, and connect it safely to EdgeSwarm. In this guide, you will learn exactly how setting up your devnet wallet works inside EdgeSwarm, why it exists, how to use it safely, and how to debug it when something goes wrong. EdgeSwarm is built on a simple promise: agents that work, proof that pays. That promise only holds if every step is verifiable, every payment is policy-checked, and every receipt can be checked by anyone later. This page is written for builders, hackers, reviewers, and judges at the Solana Hackathon who want the full picture, not just a marketing summary. Read it end to end for your first pass, then use it as a reference while you build. By the end, you will be able to explain setting up your devnet wallet to a teammate, implement it in a demo, and defend your design choices in a review.

## Why Setting Up Your Devnet Wallet Matters

Setting Up Your Devnet Wallet is not a side feature. It is a load-bearing part of the EdgeSwarm trust story. Without it, you are back to trusting a single server, a single model, or a single human claim. With it, you get a system where a job on a real edge device can be checked by a different agent on a different host, and payment only happens when both policy checks pass and verification says VERIFIED. That is the difference between a chatbot demo and a machine-to-machine economy. For getting started, the stakes are concrete: budgets are real USDC, even if they are tiny in the demo at $0.10 per job. A bug here means overspend, a tampered result getting paid, or a good worker not getting paid. This guide shows you how EdgeSwarm prevents all three. You will see the exact checks, the exact hashes, and the exact user experience that keeps the main wallet safe while the capped agent wallet does the small, bounded work.

## How Setting Up Your Devnet Wallet Works in EdgeSwarm

At a high level, EdgeSwarm always follows the same flow: a user creates a budgeted task, Policy Check 1 admits it, EdgeAgent executes it on a real device, ProofAgent independently checks it on a different host, Policy Check 2 plus Exact Message Review gates payment, Solana Devnet settles USDC, and a signed receipt is issued. Setting Up Your Devnet Wallet sits inside that flow at a precise point. In this section we unpack that point. First, the Coordinator creates a TaskEnvelopeV1 that pins the job definition, input hash, policy hash, budget in micro-USDC, expiry, and nonce. That envelope is hashed to a task hash. Any change to the envelope changes the hash. Second, the worker is assigned and executes under resource limits. Third, the worker signs the result with Ed25519 under a domain-separated context that binds job ID, assignment ID, input digest, output digest, nonce, and policy scope. Fourth, the verifier re-derives the result from trusted inputs and compares canonical bytes. Fifth, only VERIFIED pays. WARNING or REJECTED never authorizes payment. That invariant is enforced in code and in policy, not just in documentation.

### The Core Invariant: Only VERIFIED Pays

If you remember one rule from this entire docs site, remember this: only VERIFIED pays. It sounds simple, but it changes everything. It means the Coordinator cannot pay a job that failed verification, even if the worker insists it is correct. It means a tampered result, even if it looks plausible, is rejected and the reservation is released. It means a job that times out, exceeds its budget, or violates policy is not paid, and the reason is logged with a code. For setting up your devnet wallet, this invariant is checked in two places: in the Coordinator state machine, which refuses to transition a non-VERIFIED job to payment, and in Policy Check 2, which re-validates budget, policy version, and verification level before any transaction is built. In your demo, show this invariant explicitly. Create one good job that verifies and pays, and one tampered job that is rejected. Judges remember the rejected job more than the happy path, because it proves you thought about abuse.

## Step-by-Step Guide: Setting Up Your Devnet Wallet

This is the hands-on part. Follow these steps in order. Each step builds on the previous one. Do not skip the verification steps, even if your job looks correct. In EdgeSwarm, looking correct is not enough. You need proof.

**Step 1 — Define the goal for setting up your devnet wallet.** Write one sentence: what should happen, what should not happen, and how you will know it worked. For example, for job job_005_setting_up_y, the goal is to produce a result that can be re-derived by a verifier with the same inputs. Keep the goal small. A small, verifiable job beats a large, unverifiable one every time.

**Step 2 — Pin your inputs.** Hash your inputs and record the input hash. If your job uses a document, a CSV, an image, or a source URL, pin it. For GossipMarket-style jobs, pin the source snapshot. For data jobs, pin the CSV bytes. The verifier must use the same pinned inputs, not whatever the worker claims it used.

**Step 3 — Set budget and policy.** Set a budget in micro-USDC. In the demo, use $0.10, which is 100000 micro-USDC. Set caps: $0.10 per job, $1.00 per hour. Set policy version and hash. Record the policy hash in the envelope. If you change policy later, the hash changes and old envelopes are invalid.

**Step 4 — Create the TaskEnvelopeV1.** Build the envelope with jobId, inputHash, policyHash, budget, expiry, and nonce. Hash the canonical envelope to get the task hash. This task hash is your job identity. Share it in logs, in the dashboard, and in your receipt.

**Step 5 — Run Policy Check 1.** The Coordinator checks policy before any work. If the job violates budget, allowlist, quota, or expiry, it is rejected before assignment. This saves device time and money. Log the decision with policy version and reason.

**Step 6 — Assign and execute.** The Coordinator assigns a worker. EdgeAgent executes under CPU, memory, time, and battery limits. The worker signs the result. The signature binds job, assignment, digests, nonce, and policy. If the device goes offline, the job can be retried safely because the nonce and assignment make retries idempotent.

**Step 7 — Verify independently.** ProofAgent fetches the same pinned inputs, replays deterministic work, and compares canonical output bytes. It checks schema at E0, signature at E1, replay at E2, and corroboration at E3 when needed. It never trusts worker assertions. It writes a verification verdict with evidence level and rejection code if needed.

**Step 8 — Run Policy Check 2 and Exact Message Review.** After VERIFIED, Policy Check 2 re-validates budget and policy. Then the user sees the exact message to be signed: recipient, amount, memo, and job binding. The main wallet never auto-signs. Only the capped agent wallet signs, and only after human review in the demo flow.

**Step 9 — Settle on Solana.** The Coordinator builds a Solana Devnet USDC transaction, submits it, confirms it, and reconciles the reservation. Fees are about $0.0002 and settle is about 0.9 seconds in the demo. Record the transaction signature.

**Step 10 — Issue and check the receipt.** EdgeProof issues a signed receipt with task hash, result hash, worker DID, verifier DID, policy hash, and tx signature. Verify the receipt offline: check hashes, check signatures, check policy hash. Save the receipt. It is your portable proof.

## Code Example: Setting Up Your Devnet Wallet

Below is a simplified TypeScript example that shows the shape of setting up your devnet wallet in code. It is not production code, but it shows the exact fields you must get right. Copy it, adapt it to your job type, and test it on Devnet before you demo.

```pseudocode-unvalidated
// Setting Up Your Devnet Wallet — simplified EdgeSwarm example
const envelope = {
  jobId: "job_005_setting_up_y",
  inputHash: "sha256:…", // hash of pinned inputs
  policyHash: "sha256:…", // hash of policy version
  budgetMicroUsdc: 100000, // $0.10
  expiresAt: Date.now() + 10 * 60 * 1000,
  nonce: crypto.randomUUID(),
};
const taskHash = await hashCanonical(envelope);
// Policy Check 1
const admitted = await policyCheck1(envelope);
if (!admitted) throw new Error("Policy Check 1 rejected");
// Execute on EdgeAgent, sign with Ed25519
const result = await edgeAgent.execute(envelope);
// Verify with ProofAgent — never trust worker claim
const verdict = await proofAgent.verify(envelope, result);
if (verdict.status !== "VERIFIED") throw new Error(verdict.code);
// Policy Check 2 + Exact Message Review

```pseudocode-unvalidated

Notice what is missing: there is no step where the main wallet auto-signs, no step where a WARNING job pays, and no step where the Coordinator trusts the worker. Those omissions are the design. ## Real Example: Setting Up Your Devnet Wallet in a Demo

Imagine you are demoing setting up your devnet wallet for judges. You open the dashboard and create a job: “Analyze this document locally. Budget: $0.10.” The dashboard shows the envelope, the task hash, and the policy hash. You press Create. Policy Check 1 passes in milliseconds. EdgeAgent on a real Android device picks up the job. It runs under limits, signs the result, and uploads digests. ProofAgent on a different host fetches the same pinned document, replays the analysis, and matches the result. The dashboard flips to VERIFIED (E2). Policy Check 2 passes. You see the exact message: pay $0.10 USDC to worker DID for job job_005_setting_up_y. You approve with the capped agent wallet. Solana Devnet settles in about 0.9 seconds for about $0.0002. The receipt appears with all hashes and the tx signature. Then you show the tampered variant: you flip one byte in the result, the hash mismatches, verification fails with a clear code, and payment is denied. That second demo is the one judges will remember. It proves you built a system, not a slide deck.

## Best Practices for Setting Up Your Devnet Wallet

**1. Keep jobs small and deterministic.** Small jobs verify faster and replay cleanly. If your job is nondeterministic, declare it. Do not pretend a random model output is deterministic. Use E3 corroboration for nondeterministic work, and label it honestly.

**2. Pin everything.** Pin inputs, models, code version, and policy. If it is not pinned, it cannot be verified. If it cannot be verified, it cannot be paid. Pinning is not bureaucracy. It is the only way the verifier can do its job.

**3. Use integer micro-USDC everywhere.** Never use floats for money. $0.10 is 100000 micro-USDC. Store it as an integer, reserve it atomically, and reconcile it to the on-chain amount. Floats cause rounding bugs that are hard to debug and easy to exploit.

**4. Log decisions with hashes.** Log task hash, result hash, policy hash, verifier DID, and verdict for every job. Logs without hashes are stories. Logs with hashes are evidence. You will need them for audit, for debugging, and for your hackathon demo.

**5. Test the failure path.** Test tampered results, expired jobs, over-budget jobs, offline workers, and failed verifications. The happy path is easy. The failure path is where trust is built. Write a test for each rejection code and show it in your demo.

**Pitfall: Hash mismatch after a tiny edit.** You changed one character in the input and verification failed. That is correct behavior. The hash changed. Re-pin the input, create a new envelope, and re-run. Do not try to patch the old hash.

**Pitfall: Policy Check 1 passes but Check 2 fails.** Policy changed between creation and verification, or budget was already spent by a concurrent job. Check policy version, check reservations, and re-create with fresh policy hash.

**Pitfall: Verifier says WARNING.** WARNING is not VERIFIED. WARNING never pays. Read the warning code, fix the input or the verifier, and re-run. Do not force a WARNING job to pay.

**Pitfall: Payment stuck or not confirmed.** Check the transaction signature on Devnet explorer, check reservation status, and check if the reservation expired. If it expired, the reservation is released and you need a new job. Do not retry the same transaction with a new nonce without checking reconciliation.

Security for setting up your devnet wallet starts with separation. The main wallet never auto-signs. The agent wallet is capped. The worker and verifier are in separate trust boundaries. Signatures are domain-separated. Nonces and expiry prevent replay. Policy is versioned and hashed. If any of those separations break, stop and fix it. ## How Dashboard Tour: Coordinator UI Works in EdgeSwarm

At a high level, EdgeSwarm always follows the same flow: a user creates a budgeted task, Policy Check 1 admits it, EdgeAgent executes it on a real device, ProofAgent independently checks it on a different host, Policy Check 2 plus Exact Message Review gates payment, Solana Devnet settles USDC, and a signed receipt is issued. Any change to the envelope changes the hash. Second, the worker is assigned and executes under resource limits. Third, the worker signs the result with Ed25519 under a domain-separated context that binds job ID, assignment ID, input digest, output digest, nonce, and policy scope. Fourth, the verifier re-derives the result from trusted inputs and compares canonical bytes. Fifth, only VERIFIED pays. WARNING or REJECTED never authorizes payment. If you remember one rule from this entire docs site, remember this: only VERIFIED pays. It sounds simple, but it changes everything. It means a tampered result, even if it looks plausible, is rejected and the reservation is released. It means a job that times out, exceeds its budget, or violates policy is not paid, and the reason is logged with a code. # Timeouts, Expiry, and Nonces

Expiry, timeouts, and nonces prevent replay, stale jobs, and stuck reservations. In this guide, you will learn exactly how timeouts, expiry, and nonces works inside EdgeSwarm, why it exists, how to use it safely, and how to debug it when something goes wrong. EdgeSwarm is built on a simple promise: agents that work, proof that pays. That promise only holds if every step is verifiable, every payment is policy-checked, and every receipt can be checked by anyone later. This page is written for builders, hackers, reviewers, and judges at the Solana Hackathon who want the full picture, not just a marketing summary. Read it end to end for your first pass, then use it as a reference while you build. By the end, you will be able to explain timeouts, expiry, and nonces to a teammate, implement it in a demo, and defend your design choices in a review.

## Why Timeouts, Expiry, and Nonces Matters

Timeouts, Expiry, and Nonces is not a side feature. It is a load-bearing part of the EdgeSwarm trust story. Without it, you are back to trusting a single server, a single model, or a single human claim. With it, you get a system where a job on a real edge device can be checked by a different agent on a different host, and payment only happens when both policy checks pass and verification says VERIFIED. That is the difference between a chatbot demo and a machine-to-machine economy. For core concepts, the stakes are concrete: budgets are real USDC, even if they are tiny in the demo at $0.10 per job. A bug here means overspend, a tampered result getting paid, or a good worker not getting paid. This guide shows you how EdgeSwarm prevents all three. You will see the exact checks, the exact hashes, and the exact user experience that keeps the main wallet safe while the capped agent wallet does the small, bounded work.

## How Timeouts, Expiry, and Nonces Works in EdgeSwarm

At a high level, EdgeSwarm always follows the same flow: a user creates a budgeted task, Policy Check 1 admits it, EdgeAgent executes it on a real device, ProofAgent independently checks it on a different host, Policy Check 2 plus Exact Message Review gates payment, Solana Devnet settles USDC, and a signed receipt is issued. Timeouts, Expiry, and Nonces sits inside that flow at a precise point. In this section we unpack that point. First, the Coordinator creates a TaskEnvelopeV1 that pins the job definition, input hash, policy hash, budget in micro-USDC, expiry, and nonce. That envelope is hashed to a task hash. Any change to the envelope changes the hash. Second, the worker is assigned and executes under resource limits. Third, the worker signs the result with Ed25519 under a domain-separated context that binds job ID, assignment ID, input digest, output digest, nonce, and policy scope. Fourth, the verifier re-derives the result from trusted inputs and compares canonical bytes. Fifth, only VERIFIED pays. WARNING or REJECTED never authorizes payment. That invariant is enforced in code and in policy, not just in documentation.

### The Core Invariant: Only VERIFIED Pays

If you remember one rule from this entire docs site, remember this: only VERIFIED pays. It sounds simple, but it changes everything. It means the Coordinator cannot pay a job that failed verification, even if the worker insists it is correct. It means a tampered result, even if it looks plausible, is rejected and the reservation is released. It means a job that times out, exceeds its budget, or violates policy is not paid, and the reason is logged with a code. For timeouts, expiry, and nonces, this invariant is checked in two places: in the Coordinator state machine, which refuses to transition a non-VERIFIED job to payment, and in Policy Check 2, which re-validates budget, policy version, and verification level before any transaction is built. In your demo, show this invariant explicitly. Create one good job that verifies and pays, and one tampered job that is rejected. Judges remember the rejected job more than the happy path, because it proves you thought about abuse.

## Step-by-Step Guide: Timeouts, Expiry, and Nonces

This is the hands-on part. Follow these steps in order. Each step builds on the previous one. Do not skip the verification steps, even if your job looks correct. In EdgeSwarm, looking correct is not enough. You need proof.

**Step 1 — Define the goal for timeouts, expiry, and nonces.** Write one sentence: what should happen, what should not happen, and how you will know it worked. For example, for job job_020_timeouts,_ex, the goal is to produce a result that can be re-derived by a verifier with the same inputs. Keep the goal small. A small, verifiable job beats a large, unverifiable one every time.

**Step 2 — Pin your inputs.** Hash your inputs and record the input hash. If your job uses a document, a CSV, an image, or a source URL, pin it. For GossipMarket-style jobs, pin the source snapshot. For data jobs, pin the CSV bytes. The verifier must use the same pinned inputs, not whatever the worker claims it used.

**Step 3 — Set budget and policy.** Set a budget in micro-USDC. In the demo, use $0.10, which is 100000 micro-USDC. Set caps: $0.10 per job, $1.00 per hour. Set policy version and hash. Record the policy hash in the envelope. If you change policy later, the hash changes and old envelopes are invalid.

**Step 4 — Create the TaskEnvelopeV1.** Build the envelope with jobId, inputHash, policyHash, budget, expiry, and nonce. Hash the canonical envelope to get the task hash. This task hash is your job identity. Share it in logs, in the dashboard, and in your receipt.

**Step 5 — Run Policy Check 1.** The Coordinator checks policy before any work. If the job violates budget, allowlist, quota, or expiry, it is rejected before assignment. This saves device time and money. Log the decision with policy version and reason.

**Step 6 — Assign and execute.** The Coordinator assigns a worker. EdgeAgent executes under CPU, memory, time, and battery limits. The worker signs the result. The signature binds job, assignment, digests, nonce, and policy. If the device goes offline, the job can be retried safely because the nonce and assignment make retries idempotent.

**Step 7 — Verify independently.** ProofAgent fetches the same pinned inputs, replays deterministic work, and compares canonical output bytes. It checks schema at E0, signature at E1, replay at E2, and corroboration at E3 when needed. It never trusts worker assertions. It writes a verification verdict with evidence level and rejection code if needed.

**Step 8 — Run Policy Check 2 and Exact Message Review.** After VERIFIED, Policy Check 2 re-validates budget and policy. Then the user sees the exact message to be signed: recipient, amount, memo, and job binding. The main wallet never auto-signs. Only the capped agent wallet signs, and only after human review in the demo flow.

**Step 9 — Settle on Solana.** The Coordinator builds a Solana Devnet USDC transaction, submits it, confirms it, and reconciles the reservation. Fees are about $0.0002 and settle is about 0.9 seconds in the demo. Record the transaction signature.

**Step 10 — Issue and check the receipt.** EdgeProof issues a signed receipt with task hash, result hash, worker DID, verifier DID, policy hash, and tx signature. Verify the receipt offline: check hashes, check signatures, check policy hash. Save the receipt. It is your portable proof.

## Code Example: Timeouts, Expiry, and Nonces

Below is a simplified TypeScript example that shows the shape of timeouts, expiry, and nonces in code. It is not production code, but it shows the exact fields you must get right. Copy it, adapt it to your job type, and test it on Devnet before you demo.

```pseudocode-unvalidated
// Timeouts, Expiry, and Nonces — simplified EdgeSwarm example
const envelope = {
  jobId: "job_020_timeouts,_ex",
  inputHash: "sha256:…", // hash of pinned inputs
  policyHash: "sha256:…", // hash of policy version
  budgetMicroUsdc: 100000, // $0.10
  expiresAt: Date.now() + 10 * 60 * 1000,
  nonce: crypto.randomUUID(),
};
const taskHash = await hashCanonical(envelope);
// Policy Check 1
const admitted = await policyCheck1(envelope);
if (!admitted) throw new Error("Policy Check 1 rejected");
// Execute on EdgeAgent, sign with Ed25519
const result = await edgeAgent.execute(envelope);
// Verify with ProofAgent — never trust worker claim
const verdict = await proofAgent.verify(envelope, result);
if (verdict.status !== "VERIFIED") throw new Error(verdict.code);
// Policy Check 2 + Exact Message Review
await policyCheck2(envelope, verdict);
const tx = await buildSolanaPayment(envelope, verdict);
console.log("tx", tx.signature);
```pseudocode-unvalidated

Line by line: the envelope pins everything. The task hash is the identity. Policy Check 1 gates work. Execution signs the result. Verification re-derives it. Policy Check 2 gates payment. The transaction is built only after verification. If any step fails, the job stops and the reservation is released. Notice what is missing: there is no step where the main wallet auto-signs, no step where a WARNING job pays, and no step where the Coordinator trusts the worker. Those omissions are the design. When you review code, check for those omissions. If you see a path where payment happens without VERIFIED, that is a bug. Fix it before mainnet.

## Real Example: Timeouts, Expiry, and Nonces in a Demo

Imagine you are demoing timeouts, expiry, and nonces for judges. You open the dashboard and create a job: “Analyze this document locally. Budget: $0.10.” The dashboard shows the envelope, the task hash, and the policy hash. You press Create. Policy Check 1 passes in milliseconds. EdgeAgent on a real Android device picks up the job. It runs under limits, signs the result, and uploads digests. ProofAgent on a different host fetches the same pinned document, replays the analysis, and matches the result. The dashboard flips to VERIFIED (E2). Policy Check 2 passes. You see the exact message: pay $0.10 USDC to worker DID for job job_020_timeouts,_ex. You approve with the capped agent wallet. Solana Devnet settles in about 0.9 seconds for about $0.0002. The receipt appears with all hashes and the tx signature. Then you show the tampered variant: you flip one byte in the result, the hash mismatches, verification fails with a clear code, and payment is denied. That second demo is the one judges will remember. It proves you built a system, not a slide deck.

## Best Practices for Timeouts, Expiry, and Nonces

**1. Keep jobs small and deterministic.** Small jobs verify faster and replay cleanly. If your job is nondeterministic, declare it. Do not pretend a random model output is deterministic. Use E3 corroboration for nondeterministic work, and label it honestly.

**2. Pin everything.** Pin inputs, models, code version, and policy. If it is not pinned, it cannot be verified. If it cannot be verified, it cannot be paid. Pinning is not bureaucracy. It is the only way the verifier can do its job.

**3. Use integer micro-USDC everywhere.** Never use floats for money. $0.10 is 100000 micro-USDC. Store it as an integer, reserve it atomically, and reconcile it to the on-chain amount. Floats cause rounding bugs that are hard to debug and easy to exploit.

**4. Log decisions with hashes.** Log task hash, result hash, policy hash, verifier DID, and verdict for every job. Logs without hashes are stories. Logs with hashes are evidence. You will need them for audit, for debugging, and for your hackathon demo.

**5. Test the failure path.** Test tampered results, expired jobs, over-budget jobs, offline workers, and failed verifications. The happy path is easy. The failure path is where trust is built. Write a test for each rejection code and show it in your demo.

## Common Pitfalls and Troubleshooting

**Pitfall: Hash mismatch after a tiny edit.** You changed one character in the input and verification failed. That is correct behavior. The hash changed. Re-pin the input, create a new envelope, and re-run. Do not try to patch the old hash.

**Pitfall: Policy Check 1 passes but Check 2 fails.** Policy changed between creation and verification, or budget was already spent by a concurrent job. Check policy version, check reservations, and re-create with fresh policy hash.

**Pitfall: Verifier says WARNING.** WARNING is not VERIFIED. WARNING never pays. Read the warning code, fix the input or the verifier, and re-run. Do not force a WARNING job to pay.

**Pitfall: Payment stuck or not confirmed.** Check the transaction signature on Devnet explorer, check reservation status, and check if the reservation expired. If it expired, the reservation is released and you need a new job. Do not retry the same transaction with a new nonce without checking reconciliation.

**Pitfall: Agent wallet shows $0 balance.** The agent wallet is intentionally small. Fund it with a small amount, like $2.50 USDC in the demo, and check caps. If it is empty, top it up from your main wallet with human approval and exact message review. Never auto-fund from main wallet.

## Security Notes for Timeouts, Expiry, and Nonces

Security for timeouts, expiry, and nonces starts with separation. The main wallet never auto-signs. The agent wallet is capped. The worker and verifier are in separate trust boundaries. Signatures are domain-separated. Nonces and expiry prevent replay. Policy is versioned and hashed. If any of those separations break, stop and fix it. Do not ship a demo where the main wallet signs automatically, even if it is more convenient. Convenience is not worth a drained wallet. For core concepts, also think about privacy. Content never leaves the device unless the job requires it. Only hashes are anchored. If your job handles sensitive data, run it locally, pin the source, and verify the digest, not the raw content. Document what leaves the device and what stays. Judges and users will ask. Have an answer ready that matches your code.

## Checklist: Timeouts, Expiry, and Nonces

Before you call timeouts, expiry, and nonces done, check every box. If you cannot check a box, you are not done. [ ] Envelope pins inputs, policy, budget, expiry, nonce. [ ] Task hash is recorded and shown in UI. [ ] Policy Check 1 passed and is logged. [ ] Worker executed under limits and signed result. [ ] ProofAgent verified independently at stated evidence level. [ ] Policy Check 2 passed. [ ] Exact message was reviewed before signing. [ ] Main wallet never auto-signed. [ ] Agent wallet caps enforced. [ ] Payment confirmed and reconciled. [ ] Receipt issued and verified offline. [ ] Tampered variant tested and rejected. [ ] Logs contain hashes, DIDs, and verdict. If you can check all of them, you have a demo you can defend. If you cannot, fix the unchecked box first.

## FAQ: Timeouts, Expiry, and Nonces

**Q: Does timeouts, expiry, and nonces work on mainnet?** A: Horizon 1 is Devnet for the demo. Mainnet is opt-in, capped at 0.01 SOL, with exact message review and human approval. Do not move to mainnet without the checklist in the Deployment guide.

**Q: What if verification is slow?** A: Check if the job is deterministic and small. Large or nondeterministic jobs take longer to replay. Split large jobs, pin smaller inputs, and use E3 corroboration where needed. Measure replay time and show it in your demo.

**Q: Can I use timeouts, expiry, and nonces without Solana?** A: The verification and policy logic works without Solana, but settlement and receipts are designed for Solana. For the hackathon, use Solana Devnet USDC so payment is verifiable on-chain.

**Q: How do I explain timeouts, expiry, and nonces to a non-technical judge in 30 seconds?** A: Say: We create a small, budgeted job, a real device does it, a different agent checks it independently, and we only pay if it verifies. The receipt proves it. Then show the tampered job being rejected. That is the whole story in 30 seconds.

## Next Steps

You have now read the full guide for timeouts, expiry, and nonces. Next, try it. Create a job for job_020_timeouts,_ex on Devnet, run it, verify it, and check the receipt. Then break it: tamper with one byte and watch it get rejected. That pair of experiences — one success and one rejection — teaches more than any docs page. After that, read the next page in Core Concepts: it builds directly on what you learned here. If you are following the Tutorials track, jump to the tutorial that matches this concept and build it end to end. If you are preparing for the Solana Hackathon, use this page as your talking points: explain the invariant, show the hashes, show the receipt, and show the rejection. That is how you win trust, and that is how EdgeSwarm wins. The machine-to-machine economy starts with one verified job. Build yours now.

Third, the worker signs the result with Ed25519 under a domain-separated context that binds job ID, assignment ID, input digest, output digest, nonce, and policy scope. Fourth, the verifier re-derives the result from trusted inputs and compares canonical bytes. Fifth, only VERIFIED pays. WARNING or REJECTED never authorizes payment. That invariant is enforced in code and in policy, not just in documentation.

It means a tampered result, even if it looks plausible, is rejected and the reservation is released. It means a job that times out, exceeds its budget, or violates policy is not paid, and the reason is logged with a code. For coordinator deep dive, this invariant is checked in two places: in the Coordinator state machine, which refuses to transition a non-VERIFIED job to payment, and in Policy Check 2, which re-validates budget, policy version, and verification level before any transaction is built. **Step 3 — Set budget and policy.** Set a budget in micro-USDC. In the demo, use $0.10, which is 100000 micro-USDC. Set caps: $0.10 per job, $1.00 per hour. Set policy version and hash.   policyHash: "sha256:…", // hash of policy version

ProofAgent Trust Boundary is not a side feature. It is a load-bearing part of the EdgeSwarm trust story. Without it, you are back to trusting a single server, a single model, or a single human claim. With it, you get a system where a job on a real edge device can be checked by a different agent on a different host, and payment only happens when both policy checks pass and verification says VERIFIED. That is the difference between a chatbot demo and a machine-to-machine economy. For architecture, the stakes are concrete: budgets are real USDC, even if they are tiny in the demo at $0.10 per job. A bug here means overspend, a tampered result getting paid, or a good worker not getting paid. This guide shows you how EdgeSwarm prevents all three. You will see the exact checks, the exact hashes, and the exact user experience that keeps the main wallet safe while the capped agent wallet does the small, bounded work.

## How ProofAgent Trust Boundary Works in EdgeSwarm

At a high level, EdgeSwarm always follows the same flow: a user creates a budgeted task, Policy Check 1 admits it, EdgeAgent executes it on a real device, ProofAgent independently checks it on a different host, Policy Check 2 plus Exact Message Review gates payment, Solana Devnet settles USDC, and a signed receipt is issued. First, the Coordinator creates a TaskEnvelopeV1 that pins the job definition, input hash, policy hash, budget in micro-USDC, expiry, and nonce. That envelope is hashed to a task hash. Any change to the envelope changes the hash. Second, the worker is assigned and executes under resource limits. Third, the worker signs the result with Ed25519 under a domain-separated context that binds job ID, assignment ID, input digest, output digest, nonce, and policy scope. Fourth, the verifier re-derives the result from trusted inputs and compares canonical bytes. Fifth, only VERIFIED pays. WARNING or REJECTED never authorizes payment. That invariant is enforced in code and in policy, not just in documentation.

### The Core Invariant: Only VERIFIED Pays

If you remember one rule from this entire docs site, remember this: only VERIFIED pays. It sounds simple, but it changes everything. It means the Coordinator cannot pay a job that failed verification, even if the worker insists it is correct. It means a tampered result, even if it looks plausible, is rejected and the reservation is released. It means a job that times out, exceeds its budget, or violates policy is not paid, and the reason is logged with a code. For proofagent trust boundary, this invariant is checked in two places: in the Coordinator state machine, which refuses to transition a non-VERIFIED job to payment, and in Policy Check 2, which re-validates budget, policy version, and verification level before any transaction is built. In your demo, show this invariant explicitly. Create one good job that verifies and pays, and one tampered job that is rejected. Judges remember the rejected job more than the happy path, because it proves you thought about abuse.

This is the hands-on part. Follow these steps in order. Each step builds on the previous one. Do not skip the verification steps, even if your job looks correct. In EdgeSwarm, looking correct is not enough. You need proof.

**Step 1 — Define the goal for proofagent trust boundary.** Write one sentence: what should happen, what should not happen, and how you will know it worked. For example, for job job_024_proofagent_t, the goal is to produce a result that can be re-derived by a verifier with the same inputs. Keep the goal small. A small, verifiable job beats a large, unverifiable one every time.

**Step 2 — Pin your inputs.** Hash your inputs and record the input hash. If your job uses a document, a CSV, an image, or a source URL, pin it. For GossipMarket-style jobs, pin the source snapshot. **Step 3 — Set budget and policy.** Set a budget in micro-USDC. In the demo, use $0.10, which is 100000 micro-USDC. Set caps: $0.10 per job, $1.00 per hour. Set policy version and hash.   inputHash: "sha256:…", // hash of pinned inputs
  policyHash: "sha256:…", // hash of policy version
  budgetMicroUsdc: 100000, // $0.10
  expiresAt: Date.now() + 10 * 60 * 1000,
  nonce: crypto.randomUUID(),

Imagine you are demoing proofagent trust boundary for judges. You open the dashboard and create a job: “Analyze this document locally. **1. Keep jobs small and deterministic.** Small jobs verify faster and replay cleanly. If your job is nondeterministic, declare it. Do not pretend a random model output is deterministic. Use E3 corroboration for nondeterministic work, and label it honestly.

At a high level, EdgeSwarm always follows the same flow: a user creates a budgeted task, Policy Check 1 admits it, EdgeAgent executes it on a real device, ProofAgent independently checks it on a different host, Policy Check 2 plus Exact Message Review gates payment, Solana Devnet settles USDC, and a signed receipt is issued. Validate output schema, types, and digests before any deeper verification. Read it end to end for your first pass, then use it as a reference while you build. By the end, you will be able to explain schema and digest checks (e0) to a teammate, implement it in a demo, and defend your design choices in a review.

## Why Schema and Digest Checks (E0) Matters

Schema and Digest Checks (E0) is not a side feature. It is a load-bearing part of the EdgeSwarm trust story. Without it, you are back to trusting a single server, a single model, or a single human claim. With it, you get a system where a job on a real edge device can be checked by a different agent on a different host, and payment only happens when both policy checks pass and verification says VERIFIED. That is the difference between a chatbot demo and a machine-to-machine economy. For proofagent, the stakes are concrete: budgets are real USDC, even if they are tiny in the demo at $0.10 per job. A bug here means overspend, a tampered result getting paid, or a good worker not getting paid. This guide shows you how EdgeSwarm prevents all three. You will see the exact checks, the exact hashes, and the exact user experience that keeps the main wallet safe while the capped agent wallet does the small, bounded work.

## How Schema and Digest Checks (E0) Works in EdgeSwarm

At a high level, EdgeSwarm always follows the same flow: a user creates a budgeted task, Policy Check 1 admits it, EdgeAgent executes it on a real device, ProofAgent independently checks it on a different host, Policy Check 2 plus Exact Message Review gates payment, Solana Devnet settles USDC, and a signed receipt is issued. First, the Coordinator creates a TaskEnvelopeV1 that pins the job definition, input hash, policy hash, budget in micro-USDC, expiry, and nonce. That envelope is hashed to a task hash. Any change to the envelope changes the hash. Second, the worker is assigned and executes under resource limits. Third, the worker signs the result with Ed25519 under a domain-separated context that binds job ID, assignment ID, input digest, output digest, nonce, and policy scope. Fourth, the verifier re-derives the result from trusted inputs and compares canonical bytes. Fifth, only VERIFIED pays. WARNING or REJECTED never authorizes payment. That invariant is enforced in code and in policy, not just in documentation.

### The Core Invariant: Only VERIFIED Pays

If you remember one rule from this entire docs site, remember this: only VERIFIED pays. It sounds simple, but it changes everything. It means the Coordinator cannot pay a job that failed verification, even if the worker insists it is correct. It means a tampered result, even if it looks plausible, is rejected and the reservation is released. It means a job that times out, exceeds its budget, or violates policy is not paid, and the reason is logged with a code. For schema and digest checks (e0), this invariant is checked in two places: in the Coordinator state machine, which refuses to transition a non-VERIFIED job to payment, and in Policy Check 2, which re-validates budget, policy version, and verification level before any transaction is built. This is the hands-on part. Follow these steps in order. Each step builds on the previous one. Do not skip the verification steps, even if your job looks correct. In EdgeSwarm, looking correct is not enough. You need proof.

**Step 1 — Define the goal for schema and digest checks (e0).** Write one sentence: what should happen, what should not happen, and how you will know it worked. For example, for job job_043_schema_and_d, the goal is to produce a result that can be re-derived by a verifier with the same inputs. Keep the goal small. **Step 2 — Pin your inputs.** Hash your inputs and record the input hash. If your job uses a document, a CSV, an image, or a source URL, pin it. For GossipMarket-style jobs, pin the source snapshot. **Step 3 — Set budget and policy.** Set a budget in micro-USDC. In the demo, use $0.10, which is 100000 micro-USDC. Set caps: $0.10 per job, $1.00 per hour. Set policy version and hash. # Corroborating Observations (E3)

Use multiple independent observations to corroborate results when exact replay is impossible. In this guide, you will learn exactly how corroborating observations (e3) works inside EdgeSwarm, why it exists, how to use it safely, and how to debug it when something goes wrong. EdgeSwarm is built on a simple promise: agents that work, proof that pays. That promise only holds if every step is verifiable, every payment is policy-checked, and every receipt can be checked by anyone later. This page is written for builders, hackers, reviewers, and judges at the Solana Hackathon who want the full picture, not just a marketing summary. Read it end to end for your first pass, then use it as a reference while you build. By the end, you will be able to explain corroborating observations (e3) to a teammate, implement it in a demo, and defend your design choices in a review.

## Why Corroborating Observations (E3) Matters

Corroborating Observations (E3) is not a side feature. It is a load-bearing part of the EdgeSwarm trust story. Without it, you are back to trusting a single server, a single model, or a single human claim. With it, you get a system where a job on a real edge device can be checked by a different agent on a different host, and payment only happens when both policy checks pass and verification says VERIFIED. That is the difference between a chatbot demo and a machine-to-machine economy. For proofagent, the stakes are concrete: budgets are real USDC, even if they are tiny in the demo at $0.10 per job. A bug here means overspend, a tampered result getting paid, or a good worker not getting paid. This guide shows you how EdgeSwarm prevents all three. You will see the exact checks, the exact hashes, and the exact user experience that keeps the main wallet safe while the capped agent wallet does the small, bounded work.

## How Corroborating Observations (E3) Works in EdgeSwarm

At a high level, EdgeSwarm always follows the same flow: a user creates a budgeted task, Policy Check 1 admits it, EdgeAgent executes it on a real device, ProofAgent independently checks it on a different host, Policy Check 2 plus Exact Message Review gates payment, Solana Devnet settles USDC, and a signed receipt is issued. Corroborating Observations (E3) sits inside that flow at a precise point. In this section we unpack that point. First, the Coordinator creates a TaskEnvelopeV1 that pins the job definition, input hash, policy hash, budget in micro-USDC, expiry, and nonce. That envelope is hashed to a task hash. Any change to the envelope changes the hash. Second, the worker is assigned and executes under resource limits. Third, the worker signs the result with Ed25519 under a domain-separated context that binds job ID, assignment ID, input digest, output digest, nonce, and policy scope. Fourth, the verifier re-derives the result from trusted inputs and compares canonical bytes. Fifth, only VERIFIED pays. WARNING or REJECTED never authorizes payment. That invariant is enforced in code and in policy, not just in documentation.

### The Core Invariant: Only VERIFIED Pays

If you remember one rule from this entire docs site, remember this: only VERIFIED pays. It sounds simple, but it changes everything. It means the Coordinator cannot pay a job that failed verification, even if the worker insists it is correct. It means a tampered result, even if it looks plausible, is rejected and the reservation is released. It means a job that times out, exceeds its budget, or violates policy is not paid, and the reason is logged with a code. For corroborating observations (e3), this invariant is checked in two places: in the Coordinator state machine, which refuses to transition a non-VERIFIED job to payment, and in Policy Check 2, which re-validates budget, policy version, and verification level before any transaction is built. In your demo, show this invariant explicitly. Create one good job that verifies and pays, and one tampered job that is rejected. Judges remember the rejected job more than the happy path, because it proves you thought about abuse.

## Step-by-Step Guide: Corroborating Observations (E3)

This is the hands-on part. Follow these steps in order. Each step builds on the previous one. Do not skip the verification steps, even if your job looks correct. In EdgeSwarm, looking correct is not enough. You need proof.

**Step 1 — Define the goal for corroborating observations (e3).** Write one sentence: what should happen, what should not happen, and how you will know it worked. For example, for job job_045_corroboratin, the goal is to produce a result that can be re-derived by a verifier with the same inputs. Keep the goal small. A small, verifiable job beats a large, unverifiable one every time.

**Step 2 — Pin your inputs.** Hash your inputs and record the input hash. If your job uses a document, a CSV, an image, or a source URL, pin it. For GossipMarket-style jobs, pin the source snapshot. For data jobs, pin the CSV bytes. The verifier must use the same pinned inputs, not whatever the worker claims it used.

**Step 3 — Set budget and policy.** Set a budget in micro-USDC. In the demo, use $0.10, which is 100000 micro-USDC. Set caps: $0.10 per job, $1.00 per hour. Set policy version and hash. Record the policy hash in the envelope. If you change policy later, the hash changes and old envelopes are invalid.

**Step 4 — Create the TaskEnvelopeV1.** Build the envelope with jobId, inputHash, policyHash, budget, expiry, and nonce. Hash the canonical envelope to get the task hash. This task hash is your job identity. Share it in logs, in the dashboard, and in your receipt.

**Step 5 — Run Policy Check 1.** The Coordinator checks policy before any work. If the job violates budget, allowlist, quota, or expiry, it is rejected before assignment. This saves device time and money. Log the decision with policy version and reason.

**Step 7 — Verify independently.** ProofAgent fetches the same pinned inputs, replays deterministic work, and compares canonical output bytes. It checks schema at E0, signature at E1, replay at E2, and corroboration at E3 when needed. It never trusts worker assertions. It writes a verification verdict with evidence level and rejection code if needed.

**Step 8 — Run Policy Check 2 and Exact Message Review.** After VERIFIED, Policy Check 2 re-validates budget and policy. **Step 9 — Settle on Solana.** The Coordinator builds a Solana Devnet USDC transaction, submits it, confirms it, and reconciles the reservation. Fees are about $0.0002 and settle is about 0.9 seconds in the demo. Record the transaction signature.

**Step 10 — Issue and check the receipt.** EdgeProof issues a signed receipt with task hash, result hash, worker DID, verifier DID, policy hash, and tx signature. Verify the receipt offline: check hashes, check signatures, check policy hash. Save the receipt. It is your portable proof.

  inputHash: "sha256:…", // hash of pinned inputs
  policyHash: "sha256:…", // hash of policy version
  budgetMicroUsdc: 100000, // $0.10
  expiresAt: Date.now() + 10 * 60 * 1000,
  nonce: crypto.randomUUID(),

Imagine you are demoing corroborating observations (e3) for judges. You open the dashboard and create a job: “Analyze this document locally. EdgeSwarm is built on a simple promise: agents that work, proof that pays. That promise only holds if every step is verifiable, every payment is policy-checked, and every receipt can be checked by anyone later. Writing Custom Verifiers is not a side feature. It is a load-bearing part of the EdgeSwarm trust story. Without it, you are back to trusting a single server, a single model, or a single human claim. With it, you get a system where a job on a real edge device can be checked by a different agent on a different host, and payment only happens when both policy checks pass and verification says VERIFIED. That is the difference between a chatbot demo and a machine-to-machine economy. For proofagent, the stakes are concrete: budgets are real USDC, even if they are tiny in the demo at $0.10 per job. A bug here means overspend, a tampered result getting paid, or a good worker not getting paid. This guide shows you how EdgeSwarm prevents all three. You will see the exact checks, the exact hashes, and the exact user experience that keeps the main wallet safe while the capped agent wallet does the small, bounded work.

## How Writing Custom Verifiers Works in EdgeSwarm

At a high level, EdgeSwarm always follows the same flow: a user creates a budgeted task, Policy Check 1 admits it, EdgeAgent executes it on a real device, ProofAgent independently checks it on a different host, Policy Check 2 plus Exact Message Review gates payment, Solana Devnet settles USDC, and a signed receipt is issued. Writing Custom Verifiers sits inside that flow at a precise point. In this section we unpack that point. First, the Coordinator creates a TaskEnvelopeV1 that pins the job definition, input hash, policy hash, budget in micro-USDC, expiry, and nonce. That envelope is hashed to a task hash. Any change to the envelope changes the hash. Second, the worker is assigned and executes under resource limits. Third, the worker signs the result with Ed25519 under a domain-separated context that binds job ID, assignment ID, input digest, output digest, nonce, and policy scope. Fourth, the verifier re-derives the result from trusted inputs and compares canonical bytes. Fifth, only VERIFIED pays. WARNING or REJECTED never authorizes payment. That invariant is enforced in code and in policy, not just in documentation.

### The Core Invariant: Only VERIFIED Pays

If you remember one rule from this entire docs site, remember this: only VERIFIED pays. It sounds simple, but it changes everything. It means the Coordinator cannot pay a job that failed verification, even if the worker insists it is correct. It means a tampered result, even if it looks plausible, is rejected and the reservation is released. It means a job that times out, exceeds its budget, or violates policy is not paid, and the reason is logged with a code. For writing custom verifiers, this invariant is checked in two places: in the Coordinator state machine, which refuses to transition a non-VERIFIED job to payment, and in Policy Check 2, which re-validates budget, policy version, and verification level before any transaction is built. **Step 1 — Define the goal for writing custom verifiers.** Write one sentence: what should happen, what should not happen, and how you will know it worked. **Step 2 — Pin your inputs.** Hash your inputs and record the input hash. If your job uses a document, a CSV, an image, or a source URL, pin it. For GossipMarket-style jobs, pin the source snapshot. **Step 3 — Set budget and policy.** Set a budget in micro-USDC. In the demo, use $0.10, which is 100000 micro-USDC. Set caps: $0.10 per job, $1.00 per hour. Set policy version and hash. **Step 7 — Verify independently.** ProofAgent fetches the same pinned inputs, replays deterministic work, and compares canonical output bytes.   inputHash: "sha256:…", // hash of pinned inputs
  policyHash: "sha256:…", // hash of policy version
  budgetMicroUsdc: 100000, // $0.10
  expiresAt: Date.now() + 10 * 60 * 1000,
  nonce: crypto.randomUUID(),

You will see the exact checks, the exact hashes, and the exact user experience that keeps the main wallet safe while the capped agent wallet does the small, bounded work.

## How Exact Message Review: What You Sign Works in EdgeSwarm

Any change to the envelope changes the hash. Second, the worker is assigned and executes under resource limits. Fourth, the verifier re-derives the result from trusted inputs and compares canonical bytes. Fifth, only VERIFIED pays. WARNING or REJECTED never authorizes payment. That invariant is enforced in code and in policy, not just in documentation.

If you remember one rule from this entire docs site, remember this: only VERIFIED pays. It sounds simple, but it changes everything. It means the Coordinator cannot pay a job that failed verification, even if the worker insists it is correct. # Building a Payment Transaction

Build a Solana payment transaction from a verified receipt with correct accounts and memo. In this guide, you will learn exactly how building a payment transaction works inside EdgeSwarm, why it exists, how to use it safely, and how to debug it when something goes wrong. EdgeSwarm is built on a simple promise: agents that work, proof that pays. That promise only holds if every step is verifiable, every payment is policy-checked, and every receipt can be checked by anyone later. This page is written for builders, hackers, reviewers, and judges at the Solana Hackathon who want the full picture, not just a marketing summary. Read it end to end for your first pass, then use it as a reference while you build. By the end, you will be able to explain building a payment transaction to a teammate, implement it in a demo, and defend your design choices in a review.

## Why Building a Payment Transaction Matters

Building a Payment Transaction is not a side feature. It is a load-bearing part of the EdgeSwarm trust story. Without it, you are back to trusting a single server, a single model, or a single human claim. With it, you get a system where a job on a real edge device can be checked by a different agent on a different host, and payment only happens when both policy checks pass and verification says VERIFIED. That is the difference between a chatbot demo and a machine-to-machine economy. For solana settlement, the stakes are concrete: budgets are real USDC, even if they are tiny in the demo at $0.10 per job. A bug here means overspend, a tampered result getting paid, or a good worker not getting paid. This guide shows you how EdgeSwarm prevents all three. You will see the exact checks, the exact hashes, and the exact user experience that keeps the main wallet safe while the capped agent wallet does the small, bounded work.

## How Building a Payment Transaction Works in EdgeSwarm

At a high level, EdgeSwarm always follows the same flow: a user creates a budgeted task, Policy Check 1 admits it, EdgeAgent executes it on a real device, ProofAgent independently checks it on a different host, Policy Check 2 plus Exact Message Review gates payment, Solana Devnet settles USDC, and a signed receipt is issued. Building a Payment Transaction sits inside that flow at a precise point. In this section we unpack that point. First, the Coordinator creates a TaskEnvelopeV1 that pins the job definition, input hash, policy hash, budget in micro-USDC, expiry, and nonce. That envelope is hashed to a task hash. Any change to the envelope changes the hash. Second, the worker is assigned and executes under resource limits. Third, the worker signs the result with Ed25519 under a domain-separated context that binds job ID, assignment ID, input digest, output digest, nonce, and policy scope. Fourth, the verifier re-derives the result from trusted inputs and compares canonical bytes. Fifth, only VERIFIED pays. WARNING or REJECTED never authorizes payment. That invariant is enforced in code and in policy, not just in documentation.

### The Core Invariant: Only VERIFIED Pays

If you remember one rule from this entire docs site, remember this: only VERIFIED pays. It sounds simple, but it changes everything. It means the Coordinator cannot pay a job that failed verification, even if the worker insists it is correct. It means a tampered result, even if it looks plausible, is rejected and the reservation is released. It means a job that times out, exceeds its budget, or violates policy is not paid, and the reason is logged with a code. For building a payment transaction, this invariant is checked in two places: in the Coordinator state machine, which refuses to transition a non-VERIFIED job to payment, and in Policy Check 2, which re-validates budget, policy version, and verification level before any transaction is built. In your demo, show this invariant explicitly. Create one good job that verifies and pays, and one tampered job that is rejected. Judges remember the rejected job more than the happy path, because it proves you thought about abuse.

## Step-by-Step Guide: Building a Payment Transaction

This is the hands-on part. Follow these steps in order. Each step builds on the previous one. Do not skip the verification steps, even if your job looks correct. In EdgeSwarm, looking correct is not enough. You need proof.

**Step 1 — Define the goal for building a payment transaction.** Write one sentence: what should happen, what should not happen, and how you will know it worked. For example, for job job_066_building_a_p, the goal is to produce a result that can be re-derived by a verifier with the same inputs. Keep the goal small. A small, verifiable job beats a large, unverifiable one every time.

**Step 2 — Pin your inputs.** Hash your inputs and record the input hash. If your job uses a document, a CSV, an image, or a source URL, pin it. For GossipMarket-style jobs, pin the source snapshot. For data jobs, pin the CSV bytes. The verifier must use the same pinned inputs, not whatever the worker claims it used.

**Step 3 — Set budget and policy.** Set a budget in micro-USDC. In the demo, use $0.10, which is 100000 micro-USDC. Set caps: $0.10 per job, $1.00 per hour. Set policy version and hash. Record the policy hash in the envelope. If you change policy later, the hash changes and old envelopes are invalid.

**Step 4 — Create the TaskEnvelopeV1.** Build the envelope with jobId, inputHash, policyHash, budget, expiry, and nonce. Hash the canonical envelope to get the task hash. This task hash is your job identity. Share it in logs, in the dashboard, and in your receipt.

**Step 5 — Run Policy Check 1.** The Coordinator checks policy before any work. If the job violates budget, allowlist, quota, or expiry, it is rejected before assignment. This saves device time and money. Log the decision with policy version and reason.

**Step 7 — Verify independently.** ProofAgent fetches the same pinned inputs, replays deterministic work, and compares canonical output bytes. It checks schema at E0, signature at E1, replay at E2, and corroboration at E3 when needed. It never trusts worker assertions. It writes a verification verdict with evidence level and rejection code if needed.

**Step 8 — Run Policy Check 2 and Exact Message Review.** After VERIFIED, Policy Check 2 re-validates budget and policy. **Step 9 — Settle on Solana.** The Coordinator builds a Solana Devnet USDC transaction, submits it, confirms it, and reconciles the reservation. Fees are about $0.0002 and settle is about 0.9 seconds in the demo. Record the transaction signature.

**Step 10 — Issue and check the receipt.** EdgeProof issues a signed receipt with task hash, result hash, worker DID, verifier DID, policy hash, and tx signature. Verify the receipt offline: check hashes, check signatures, check policy hash. Save the receipt. It is your portable proof.

Below is a simplified TypeScript example that shows the shape of building a payment transaction in code. It is not production code, but it shows the exact fields you must get right. Copy it, adapt it to your job type, and test it on Devnet before you demo.

  inputHash: "sha256:…", // hash of pinned inputs
  policyHash: "sha256:…", // hash of policy version
  budgetMicroUsdc: 100000, // $0.10
  expiresAt: Date.now() + 10 * 60 * 1000,
  nonce: crypto.randomUUID(),

Imagine you are demoing building a payment transaction for judges. You open the dashboard and create a job: “Analyze this document locally. **1. Keep jobs small and deterministic.** Small jobs verify faster and replay cleanly. If your job is nondeterministic, declare it. Do not pretend a random model output is deterministic. Use E3 corroboration for nondeterministic work, and label it honestly.

**2. Pin everything.** Pin inputs, models, code version, and policy. If it is not pinned, it cannot be verified. If it cannot be verified, it cannot be paid. Pinning is not bureaucracy. It is the only way the verifier can do its job.

# Handling Failed or Stuck Payments
