EdgeSwarm is built on a simple promise: agents that work, proof that pays. That promise only holds if every step is verifiable, every payment is policy-checked, and every receipt can be checked by anyone later. This page is written for builders, hackers, reviewers, and judges at the Solana Hackathon who want the full picture, not just a marketing summary. Read it end to end for your first pass, then use it as a reference while you build. By the end, you will be able to explain handling failed or stuck payments to a teammate, implement it in a demo, and defend your design choices in a review.

## Why Handling Failed or Stuck Payments Matters

Handling Failed or Stuck Payments is not a side feature. It is a load-bearing part of the EdgeSwarm trust story. Without it, you are back to trusting a single server, a single model, or a single human claim. With it, you get a system where a job on a real edge device can be checked by a different agent on a different host, and payment only happens when both policy checks pass and verification says VERIFIED. That is the difference between a chatbot demo and a machine-to-machine economy. For solana settlement, the stakes are concrete: budgets are real USDC, even if they are tiny in the demo at $0.10 per job. A bug here means overspend, a tampered result getting paid, or a good worker not getting paid. This guide shows you how EdgeSwarm prevents all three. You will see the exact checks, the exact hashes, and the exact user experience that keeps the main wallet safe while the capped agent wallet does the small, bounded work.

## How Handling Failed or Stuck Payments Works in EdgeSwarm

At a high level, EdgeSwarm always follows the same flow: a user creates a budgeted task, Policy Check 1 admits it, EdgeAgent executes it on a real device, ProofAgent independently checks it on a different host, Policy Check 2 plus Exact Message Review gates payment, Solana Devnet settles USDC, and a signed receipt is issued. Handling Failed or Stuck Payments sits inside that flow at a precise point. In this section we unpack that point. First, the Coordinator creates a TaskEnvelopeV1 that pins the job definition, input hash, policy hash, budget in micro-USDC, expiry, and nonce. That envelope is hashed to a task hash. Any change to the envelope changes the hash. Second, the worker is assigned and executes under resource limits. Third, the worker signs the result with Ed25519 under a domain-separated context that binds job ID, assignment ID, input digest, output digest, nonce, and policy scope. Fourth, the verifier re-derives the result from trusted inputs and compares canonical bytes. Fifth, only VERIFIED pays. WARNING or REJECTED never authorizes payment. That invariant is enforced in code and in policy, not just in documentation.

### The Core Invariant: Only VERIFIED Pays

If you remember one rule from this entire docs site, remember this: only VERIFIED pays. It sounds simple, but it changes everything. It means the Coordinator cannot pay a job that failed verification, even if the worker insists it is correct. It means a tampered result, even if it looks plausible, is rejected and the reservation is released. It means a job that times out, exceeds its budget, or violates policy is not paid, and the reason is logged with a code. For handling failed or stuck payments, this invariant is checked in two places: in the Coordinator state machine, which refuses to transition a non-VERIFIED job to payment, and in Policy Check 2, which re-validates budget, policy version, and verification level before any transaction is built. In your demo, show this invariant explicitly. Create one good job that verifies and pays, and one tampered job that is rejected. **Step 3 — Set budget and policy.** Set a budget in micro-USDC. In the demo, use $0.10, which is 100000 micro-USDC. Set caps: $0.10 per job, $1.00 per hour. Set policy version and hash. Record the policy hash in the envelope. If you change policy later, the hash changes and old envelopes are invalid.

**Step 4 — Create the TaskEnvelopeV1.** Build the envelope with jobId, inputHash, policyHash, budget, expiry, and nonce. Hash the canonical envelope to get the task hash. This task hash is your job identity. Share it in logs, in the dashboard, and in your receipt.

**Step 5 — Run Policy Check 1.** The Coordinator checks policy before any work. If the job violates budget, allowlist, quota, or expiry, it is rejected before assignment. This saves device time and money. Log the decision with policy version and reason.

**Step 6 — Assign and execute.** The Coordinator assigns a worker. EdgeAgent executes under CPU, memory, time, and battery limits. The worker signs the result. **Step 8 — Run Policy Check 2 and Exact Message Review.** After VERIFIED, Policy Check 2 re-validates budget and policy. # Replay Protection and Nonce Management

Nonces, expiry, and domain separation stop replay attacks. In this guide, you will learn exactly how replay protection and nonce management works inside EdgeSwarm, why it exists, how to use it safely, and how to debug it when something goes wrong. EdgeSwarm is built on a simple promise: agents that work, proof that pays. That promise only holds if every step is verifiable, every payment is policy-checked, and every receipt can be checked by anyone later. This page is written for builders, hackers, reviewers, and judges at the Solana Hackathon who want the full picture, not just a marketing summary. Read it end to end for your first pass, then use it as a reference while you build. By the end, you will be able to explain replay protection and nonce management to a teammate, implement it in a demo, and defend your design choices in a review.

## Why Replay Protection and Nonce Management Matters

Replay Protection and Nonce Management is not a side feature. It is a load-bearing part of the EdgeSwarm trust story. Without it, you are back to trusting a single server, a single model, or a single human claim. With it, you get a system where a job on a real edge device can be checked by a different agent on a different host, and payment only happens when both policy checks pass and verification says VERIFIED. That is the difference between a chatbot demo and a machine-to-machine economy. For security, the stakes are concrete: budgets are real USDC, even if they are tiny in the demo at $0.10 per job. A bug here means overspend, a tampered result getting paid, or a good worker not getting paid. This guide shows you how EdgeSwarm prevents all three. You will see the exact checks, the exact hashes, and the exact user experience that keeps the main wallet safe while the capped agent wallet does the small, bounded work.

## How Replay Protection and Nonce Management Works in EdgeSwarm

At a high level, EdgeSwarm always follows the same flow: a user creates a budgeted task, Policy Check 1 admits it, EdgeAgent executes it on a real device, ProofAgent independently checks it on a different host, Policy Check 2 plus Exact Message Review gates payment, Solana Devnet settles USDC, and a signed receipt is issued. Replay Protection and Nonce Management sits inside that flow at a precise point. In this section we unpack that point. First, the Coordinator creates a TaskEnvelopeV1 that pins the job definition, input hash, policy hash, budget in micro-USDC, expiry, and nonce. That envelope is hashed to a task hash. Any change to the envelope changes the hash. Second, the worker is assigned and executes under resource limits. Third, the worker signs the result with Ed25519 under a domain-separated context that binds job ID, assignment ID, input digest, output digest, nonce, and policy scope. Fourth, the verifier re-derives the result from trusted inputs and compares canonical bytes. Fifth, only VERIFIED pays. WARNING or REJECTED never authorizes payment. That invariant is enforced in code and in policy, not just in documentation.

### The Core Invariant: Only VERIFIED Pays

If you remember one rule from this entire docs site, remember this: only VERIFIED pays. It sounds simple, but it changes everything. It means the Coordinator cannot pay a job that failed verification, even if the worker insists it is correct. It means a tampered result, even if it looks plausible, is rejected and the reservation is released. It means a job that times out, exceeds its budget, or violates policy is not paid, and the reason is logged with a code. For replay protection and nonce management, this invariant is checked in two places: in the Coordinator state machine, which refuses to transition a non-VERIFIED job to payment, and in Policy Check 2, which re-validates budget, policy version, and verification level before any transaction is built. In your demo, show this invariant explicitly. Create one good job that verifies and pays, and one tampered job that is rejected. Judges remember the rejected job more than the happy path, because it proves you thought about abuse.

## Step-by-Step Guide: Replay Protection and Nonce Management

This is the hands-on part. Follow these steps in order. Each step builds on the previous one. Do not skip the verification steps, even if your job looks correct. In EdgeSwarm, looking correct is not enough. You need proof.

**Step 1 — Define the goal for replay protection and nonce management.** Write one sentence: what should happen, what should not happen, and how you will know it worked. For example, for job job_083_replay_prote, the goal is to produce a result that can be re-derived by a verifier with the same inputs. Keep the goal small. A small, verifiable job beats a large, unverifiable one every time.

**Step 2 — Pin your inputs.** Hash your inputs and record the input hash. If your job uses a document, a CSV, an image, or a source URL, pin it. For GossipMarket-style jobs, pin the source snapshot. For data jobs, pin the CSV bytes. The verifier must use the same pinned inputs, not whatever the worker claims it used.

**Step 3 — Set budget and policy.** Set a budget in micro-USDC. In the demo, use $0.10, which is 100000 micro-USDC. Set caps: $0.10 per job, $1.00 per hour. Set policy version and hash. Record the policy hash in the envelope. If you change policy later, the hash changes and old envelopes are invalid.

**Step 4 — Create the TaskEnvelopeV1.** Build the envelope with jobId, inputHash, policyHash, budget, expiry, and nonce. Hash the canonical envelope to get the task hash. This task hash is your job identity. Share it in logs, in the dashboard, and in your receipt.

**Step 5 — Run Policy Check 1.** The Coordinator checks policy before any work. If the job violates budget, allowlist, quota, or expiry, it is rejected before assignment. This saves device time and money. Log the decision with policy version and reason.

**Step 6 — Assign and execute.** The Coordinator assigns a worker. EdgeAgent executes under CPU, memory, time, and battery limits. The worker signs the result. The signature binds job, assignment, digests, nonce, and policy. If the device goes offline, the job can be retried safely because the nonce and assignment make retries idempotent.

**Step 7 — Verify independently.** ProofAgent fetches the same pinned inputs, replays deterministic work, and compares canonical output bytes. It checks schema at E0, signature at E1, replay at E2, and corroboration at E3 when needed. It never trusts worker assertions. It writes a verification verdict with evidence level and rejection code if needed.

**Step 8 — Run Policy Check 2 and Exact Message Review.** After VERIFIED, Policy Check 2 re-validates budget and policy. Then the user sees the exact message to be signed: recipient, amount, memo, and job binding. The main wallet never auto-signs. Only the capped agent wallet signs, and only after human review in the demo flow.

**Step 9 — Settle on Solana.** The Coordinator builds a Solana Devnet USDC transaction, submits it, confirms it, and reconciles the reservation. Fees are about $0.0002 and settle is about 0.9 seconds in the demo. Record the transaction signature.

**Step 10 — Issue and check the receipt.** EdgeProof issues a signed receipt with task hash, result hash, worker DID, verifier DID, policy hash, and tx signature. Verify the receipt offline: check hashes, check signatures, check policy hash. Save the receipt. It is your portable proof.

## Code Example: Replay Protection and Nonce Management

Below is a simplified TypeScript example that shows the shape of replay protection and nonce management in code. It is not production code, but it shows the exact fields you must get right. Copy it, adapt it to your job type, and test it on Devnet before you demo.

```pseudocode-unvalidated
// Replay Protection and Nonce Management — simplified EdgeSwarm example
const envelope = {

  inputHash: "sha256:…", // hash of pinned inputs
  policyHash: "sha256:…", // hash of policy version
  budgetMicroUsdc: 100000, // $0.10
  expiresAt: Date.now() + 10 * 60 * 1000,
  nonce: crypto.randomUUID(),
};

// Policy Check 1
const admitted = await policyCheck1(envelope);

const result = await edgeAgent.execute(envelope);

const verdict = await proofAgent.verify(envelope, result);

// Policy Check 2 + Exact Message Review

## Real Example: Replay Protection and Nonce Management in a Demo

Imagine you are demoing replay protection and nonce management for judges. You open the dashboard and create a job: “Analyze this document locally. Budget: $0.10.” The dashboard shows the envelope, the task hash, and the policy hash. You press Create. Policy Check 1 passes in milliseconds. EdgeAgent on a real Android device picks up the job. It runs under limits, signs the result, and uploads digests. ProofAgent on a different host fetches the same pinned document, replays the analysis, and matches the result. The dashboard flips to VERIFIED (E2). Policy Check 2 passes. You see the exact message: pay $0.10 USDC to worker DID for job job_083_replay_prote. You approve with the capped agent wallet. Solana Devnet settles in about 0.9 seconds for about $0.0002. The receipt appears with all hashes and the tx signature. Then you show the tampered variant: you flip one byte in the result, the hash mismatches, verification fails with a clear code, and payment is denied. That second demo is the one judges will remember. It proves you built a system, not a slide deck.

## Best Practices for Replay Protection and Nonce Management

**1. Keep jobs small and deterministic.** Small jobs verify faster and replay cleanly. If your job is nondeterministic, declare it. Do not pretend a random model output is deterministic. Use E3 corroboration for nondeterministic work, and label it honestly.

**2. Pin everything.** Pin inputs, models, code version, and policy. If it is not pinned, it cannot be verified. If it cannot be verified, it cannot be paid. Pinning is not bureaucracy. It is the only way the verifier can do its job.

**3. Use integer micro-USDC everywhere.** Never use floats for money. $0.10 is 100000 micro-USDC. Store it as an integer, reserve it atomically, and reconcile it to the on-chain amount. Floats cause rounding bugs that are hard to debug and easy to exploit.

**4. Log decisions with hashes.** Log task hash, result hash, policy hash, verifier DID, and verdict for every job. Logs without hashes are stories. Logs with hashes are evidence. You will need them for audit, for debugging, and for your hackathon demo.

**5. Test the failure path.** Test tampered results, expired jobs, over-budget jobs, offline workers, and failed verifications. The happy path is easy. The failure path is where trust is built. Write a test for each rejection code and show it in your demo.

## Common Pitfalls and Troubleshooting

**Pitfall: Hash mismatch after a tiny edit.** You changed one character in the input and verification failed. That is correct behavior. The hash changed. Re-pin the input, create a new envelope, and re-run. Do not try to patch the old hash.

**Pitfall: Policy Check 1 passes but Check 2 fails.** Policy changed between creation and verification, or budget was already spent by a concurrent job. Check policy version, check reservations, and re-create with fresh policy hash.

**Pitfall: Verifier says WARNING.** WARNING is not VERIFIED. WARNING never pays. Read the warning code, fix the input or the verifier, and re-run. Do not force a WARNING job to pay.

**Pitfall: Payment stuck or not confirmed.** Check the transaction signature on Devnet explorer, check reservation status, and check if the reservation expired. Before you call replay protection and nonce management done, check every box. If you cannot check a box, you are not done. [ ] Envelope pins inputs, policy, budget, expiry, nonce. [ ] Policy Check 2 passed. [ ] Exact message was reviewed before signing. [ ] Main wallet never auto-signed. [ ] Agent wallet caps enforced. [ ] Payment confirmed and reconciled. The receipt proves it. Then show the tampered job being rejected. That is the whole story in 30 seconds.

# Auditing and Logging for Compliance

Log jobs, policy decisions, verifications, and payments for audit. In this guide, you will learn exactly how auditing and logging for compliance works inside EdgeSwarm, why it exists, how to use it safely, and how to debug it when something goes wrong. EdgeSwarm is built on a simple promise: agents that work, proof that pays. That promise only holds if every step is verifiable, every payment is policy-checked, and every receipt can be checked by anyone later. This page is written for builders, hackers, reviewers, and judges at the Solana Hackathon who want the full picture, not just a marketing summary. Read it end to end for your first pass, then use it as a reference while you build. By the end, you will be able to explain auditing and logging for compliance to a teammate, implement it in a demo, and defend your design choices in a review.

## Why Auditing and Logging for Compliance Matters

Auditing and Logging for Compliance is not a side feature. It is a load-bearing part of the EdgeSwarm trust story. Without it, you are back to trusting a single server, a single model, or a single human claim. With it, you get a system where a job on a real edge device can be checked by a different agent on a different host, and payment only happens when both policy checks pass and verification says VERIFIED. That is the difference between a chatbot demo and a machine-to-machine economy. For security, the stakes are concrete: budgets are real USDC, even if they are tiny in the demo at $0.10 per job. A bug here means overspend, a tampered result getting paid, or a good worker not getting paid. This guide shows you how EdgeSwarm prevents all three. You will see the exact checks, the exact hashes, and the exact user experience that keeps the main wallet safe while the capped agent wallet does the small, bounded work.

## How Auditing and Logging for Compliance Works in EdgeSwarm

At a high level, EdgeSwarm always follows the same flow: a user creates a budgeted task, Policy Check 1 admits it, EdgeAgent executes it on a real device, ProofAgent independently checks it on a different host, Policy Check 2 plus Exact Message Review gates payment, Solana Devnet settles USDC, and a signed receipt is issued. Auditing and Logging for Compliance sits inside that flow at a precise point. In this section we unpack that point. First, the Coordinator creates a TaskEnvelopeV1 that pins the job definition, input hash, policy hash, budget in micro-USDC, expiry, and nonce. That envelope is hashed to a task hash. Any change to the envelope changes the hash. Second, the worker is assigned and executes under resource limits. Third, the worker signs the result with Ed25519 under a domain-separated context that binds job ID, assignment ID, input digest, output digest, nonce, and policy scope. Fourth, the verifier re-derives the result from trusted inputs and compares canonical bytes. Fifth, only VERIFIED pays. WARNING or REJECTED never authorizes payment. That invariant is enforced in code and in policy, not just in documentation.

### The Core Invariant: Only VERIFIED Pays

If you remember one rule from this entire docs site, remember this: only VERIFIED pays. It sounds simple, but it changes everything. It means the Coordinator cannot pay a job that failed verification, even if the worker insists it is correct. It means a tampered result, even if it looks plausible, is rejected and the reservation is released. It means a job that times out, exceeds its budget, or violates policy is not paid, and the reason is logged with a code. For auditing and logging for compliance, this invariant is checked in two places: in the Coordinator state machine, which refuses to transition a non-VERIFIED job to payment, and in Policy Check 2, which re-validates budget, policy version, and verification level before any transaction is built. In your demo, show this invariant explicitly. Create one good job that verifies and pays, and one tampered job that is rejected. Judges remember the rejected job more than the happy path, because it proves you thought about abuse.

## Step-by-Step Guide: Auditing and Logging for Compliance

This is the hands-on part. Follow these steps in order. Each step builds on the previous one. Do not skip the verification steps, even if your job looks correct. In EdgeSwarm, looking correct is not enough. You need proof.

**Step 1 — Define the goal for auditing and logging for compliance.** Write one sentence: what should happen, what should not happen, and how you will know it worked. For example, for job job_087_auditing_and, the goal is to produce a result that can be re-derived by a verifier with the same inputs. Keep the goal small. A small, verifiable job beats a large, unverifiable one every time.

**Step 2 — Pin your inputs.** Hash your inputs and record the input hash. If your job uses a document, a CSV, an image, or a source URL, pin it. For GossipMarket-style jobs, pin the source snapshot. For data jobs, pin the CSV bytes. The verifier must use the same pinned inputs, not whatever the worker claims it used.

**Step 3 — Set budget and policy.** Set a budget in micro-USDC. In the demo, use $0.10, which is 100000 micro-USDC. Set caps: $0.10 per job, $1.00 per hour. Set policy version and hash. Record the policy hash in the envelope. If you change policy later, the hash changes and old envelopes are invalid.

**Step 4 — Create the TaskEnvelopeV1.** Build the envelope with jobId, inputHash, policyHash, budget, expiry, and nonce. Hash the canonical envelope to get the task hash. This task hash is your job identity. Share it in logs, in the dashboard, and in your receipt.

**Step 5 — Run Policy Check 1.** The Coordinator checks policy before any work. If the job violates budget, allowlist, quota, or expiry, it is rejected before assignment. This saves device time and money. Log the decision with policy version and reason.

**Step 6 — Assign and execute.** The Coordinator assigns a worker. EdgeAgent executes under CPU, memory, time, and battery limits. The worker signs the result. The signature binds job, assignment, digests, nonce, and policy. If the device goes offline, the job can be retried safely because the nonce and assignment make retries idempotent.

**Step 7 — Verify independently.** ProofAgent fetches the same pinned inputs, replays deterministic work, and compares canonical output bytes. It checks schema at E0, signature at E1, replay at E2, and corroboration at E3 when needed. It never trusts worker assertions. It writes a verification verdict with evidence level and rejection code if needed.

**Step 8 — Run Policy Check 2 and Exact Message Review.** After VERIFIED, Policy Check 2 re-validates budget and policy. Then the user sees the exact message to be signed: recipient, amount, memo, and job binding. The main wallet never auto-signs. Only the capped agent wallet signs, and only after human review in the demo flow.

**Step 9 — Settle on Solana.** The Coordinator builds a Solana Devnet USDC transaction, submits it, confirms it, and reconciles the reservation. Fees are about $0.0002 and settle is about 0.9 seconds in the demo. Record the transaction signature.

**Step 10 — Issue and check the receipt.** EdgeProof issues a signed receipt with task hash, result hash, worker DID, verifier DID, policy hash, and tx signature. Verify the receipt offline: check hashes, check signatures, check policy hash. Save the receipt. It is your portable proof.

Below is a simplified TypeScript example that shows the shape of auditing and logging for compliance in code. It is not production code, but it shows the exact fields you must get right. Copy it, adapt it to your job type, and test it on Devnet before you demo.

// Auditing and Logging for Compliance — simplified EdgeSwarm example

  inputHash: "sha256:…", // hash of pinned inputs
  policyHash: "sha256:…", // hash of policy version
  budgetMicroUsdc: 100000, // $0.10
  expiresAt: Date.now() + 10 * 60 * 1000,
  nonce: crypto.randomUUID(),
};

// Policy Check 1
const admitted = await policyCheck1(envelope);
if (!admitted) throw new Error("Policy Check 1 rejected");
// Execute on EdgeAgent, sign with Ed25519
const result = await edgeAgent.execute(envelope);
// Verify with ProofAgent — never trust worker claim
const verdict = await proofAgent.verify(envelope, result);

// Policy Check 2 + Exact Message Review

```pseudocode-unvalidated

## Real Example: Auditing and Logging for Compliance in a Demo

Imagine you are demoing auditing and logging for compliance for judges. You open the dashboard and create a job: “Analyze this document locally. Budget: $0.10.” The dashboard shows the envelope, the task hash, and the policy hash. You press Create. Policy Check 1 passes in milliseconds. EdgeAgent on a real Android device picks up the job. It runs under limits, signs the result, and uploads digests. ProofAgent on a different host fetches the same pinned document, replays the analysis, and matches the result. The dashboard flips to VERIFIED (E2). Policy Check 2 passes. You see the exact message: pay $0.10 USDC to worker DID for job job_087_auditing_and. You approve with the capped agent wallet. Solana Devnet settles in about 0.9 seconds for about $0.0002. The receipt appears with all hashes and the tx signature. Then you show the tampered variant: you flip one byte in the result, the hash mismatches, verification fails with a clear code, and payment is denied. That second demo is the one judges will remember. It proves you built a system, not a slide deck.

**1. Keep jobs small and deterministic.** Small jobs verify faster and replay cleanly. If your job is nondeterministic, declare it. Do not pretend a random model output is deterministic. Use E3 corroboration for nondeterministic work, and label it honestly.

**2. Pin everything.** Pin inputs, models, code version, and policy. If it is not pinned, it cannot be verified. If it cannot be verified, it cannot be paid. Pinning is not bureaucracy. It is the only way the verifier can do its job.

**3. Use integer micro-USDC everywhere.** Never use floats for money. $0.10 is 100000 micro-USDC. Store it as an integer, reserve it atomically, and reconcile it to the on-chain amount. Floats cause rounding bugs that are hard to debug and easy to exploit.

**4. Log decisions with hashes.** Log task hash, result hash, policy hash, verifier DID, and verdict for every job. Logs without hashes are stories. Logs with hashes are evidence. You will need them for audit, for debugging, and for your hackathon demo.

**5. Test the failure path.** Test tampered results, expired jobs, over-budget jobs, offline workers, and failed verifications. The happy path is easy. The failure path is where trust is built. Write a test for each rejection code and show it in your demo.

**Pitfall: Policy Check 1 passes but Check 2 fails.** Policy changed between creation and verification, or budget was already spent by a concurrent job. Check policy version, check reservations, and re-create with fresh policy hash.

**Pitfall: Verifier says WARNING.** WARNING is not VERIFIED. WARNING never pays. Read the warning code, fix the input or the verifier, and re-run. Do not force a WARNING job to pay.

**Pitfall: Payment stuck or not confirmed.** Check the transaction signature on Devnet explorer, check reservation status, and check if the reservation expired. If it expired, the reservation is released and you need a new job. Do not retry the same transaction with a new nonce without checking reconciliation.

**Pitfall: Agent wallet shows $0 balance.** The agent wallet is intentionally small. Fund it with a small amount, like $2.50 USDC in the demo, and check caps. If it is empty, top it up from your main wallet with human approval and exact message review. Never auto-fund from main wallet.

Security for auditing and logging for compliance starts with separation. The main wallet never auto-signs. The agent wallet is capped. The worker and verifier are in separate trust boundaries. Signatures are domain-separated. Nonces and expiry prevent replay. Policy is versioned and hashed. If any of those separations break, stop and fix it. That promise only holds if every step is verifiable, every payment is policy-checked, and every receipt can be checked by anyone later. By the end, you will be able to explain privacy: what never leaves device to a teammate, implement it in a demo, and defend your design choices in a review.

## Why Privacy: What Never Leaves Device Matters

Privacy: What Never Leaves Device is not a side feature. It is a load-bearing part of the EdgeSwarm trust story. Without it, you are back to trusting a single server, a single model, or a single human claim. With it, you get a system where a job on a real edge device can be checked by a different agent on a different host, and payment only happens when both policy checks pass and verification says VERIFIED. That is the difference between a chatbot demo and a machine-to-machine economy. For security, the stakes are concrete: budgets are real USDC, even if they are tiny in the demo at $0.10 per job. A bug here means overspend, a tampered result getting paid, or a good worker not getting paid. This guide shows you how EdgeSwarm prevents all three. You will see the exact checks, the exact hashes, and the exact user experience that keeps the main wallet safe while the capped agent wallet does the small, bounded work.

## How Privacy: What Never Leaves Device Works in EdgeSwarm

At a high level, EdgeSwarm always follows the same flow: a user creates a budgeted task, Policy Check 1 admits it, EdgeAgent executes it on a real device, ProofAgent independently checks it on a different host, Policy Check 2 plus Exact Message Review gates payment, Solana Devnet settles USDC, and a signed receipt is issued. Privacy: What Never Leaves Device sits inside that flow at a precise point. In this section we unpack that point. First, the Coordinator creates a TaskEnvelopeV1 that pins the job definition, input hash, policy hash, budget in micro-USDC, expiry, and nonce. That envelope is hashed to a task hash. Any change to the envelope changes the hash. Second, the worker is assigned and executes under resource limits. Third, the worker signs the result with Ed25519 under a domain-separated context that binds job ID, assignment ID, input digest, output digest, nonce, and policy scope. Fourth, the verifier re-derives the result from trusted inputs and compares canonical bytes. Fifth, only VERIFIED pays. WARNING or REJECTED never authorizes payment. That invariant is enforced in code and in policy, not just in documentation.

### The Core Invariant: Only VERIFIED Pays

If you remember one rule from this entire docs site, remember this: only VERIFIED pays. It sounds simple, but it changes everything. It means the Coordinator cannot pay a job that failed verification, even if the worker insists it is correct. It means a tampered result, even if it looks plausible, is rejected and the reservation is released. It means a job that times out, exceeds its budget, or violates policy is not paid, and the reason is logged with a code. For privacy: what never leaves device, this invariant is checked in two places: in the Coordinator state machine, which refuses to transition a non-VERIFIED job to payment, and in Policy Check 2, which re-validates budget, policy version, and verification level before any transaction is built. In your demo, show this invariant explicitly. Create one good job that verifies and pays, and one tampered job that is rejected. ## How Tutorial: Submit to Solana Hackathon on MLH Works in EdgeSwarm

At a high level, EdgeSwarm always follows the same flow: a user creates a budgeted task, Policy Check 1 admits it, EdgeAgent executes it on a real device, ProofAgent independently checks it on a different host, Policy Check 2 plus Exact Message Review gates payment, Solana Devnet settles USDC, and a signed receipt is issued. Tutorial: Submit to Solana Hackathon on MLH sits inside that flow at a precise point. In this section we unpack that point. First, the Coordinator creates a TaskEnvelopeV1 that pins the job definition, input hash, policy hash, budget in micro-USDC, expiry, and nonce. That envelope is hashed to a task hash. Any change to the envelope changes the hash. Second, the worker is assigned and executes under resource limits. Third, the worker signs the result with Ed25519 under a domain-separated context that binds job ID, assignment ID, input digest, output digest, nonce, and policy scope. Fourth, the verifier re-derives the result from trusted inputs and compares canonical bytes. Fifth, only VERIFIED pays. WARNING or REJECTED never authorizes payment. That invariant is enforced in code and in policy, not just in documentation.

### The Core Invariant: Only VERIFIED Pays

If you remember one rule from this entire docs site, remember this: only VERIFIED pays. It sounds simple, but it changes everything. It means the Coordinator cannot pay a job that failed verification, even if the worker insists it is correct. It means a tampered result, even if it looks plausible, is rejected and the reservation is released. It means a job that times out, exceeds its budget, or violates policy is not paid, and the reason is logged with a code. For tutorial: submit to solana hackathon on mlh, this invariant is checked in two places: in the Coordinator state machine, which refuses to transition a non-VERIFIED job to payment, and in Policy Check 2, which re-validates budget, policy version, and verification level before any transaction is built. In your demo, show this invariant explicitly. Create one good job that verifies and pays, and one tampered job that is rejected. Judges remember the rejected job more than the happy path, because it proves you thought about abuse.

## Step-by-Step Guide: Tutorial: Submit to Solana Hackathon on MLH

This is the hands-on part. Follow these steps in order. Each step builds on the previous one. Do not skip the verification steps, even if your job looks correct. In EdgeSwarm, looking correct is not enough. You need proof.

**Step 1 — Define the goal for tutorial: submit to solana hackathon on mlh.** Write one sentence: what should happen, what should not happen, and how you will know it worked. For example, for job job_100_tutorial:_su, the goal is to produce a result that can be re-derived by a verifier with the same inputs. Keep the goal small. A small, verifiable job beats a large, unverifiable one every time.

**Step 2 — Pin your inputs.** Hash your inputs and record the input hash. If your job uses a document, a CSV, an image, or a source URL, pin it. For GossipMarket-style jobs, pin the source snapshot. For data jobs, pin the CSV bytes. The verifier must use the same pinned inputs, not whatever the worker claims it used.

**Step 3 — Set budget and policy.** Set a budget in micro-USDC. In the demo, use $0.10, which is 100000 micro-USDC. Set caps: $0.10 per job, $1.00 per hour. Set policy version and hash. Record the policy hash in the envelope. If you change policy later, the hash changes and old envelopes are invalid.

**Step 4 — Create the TaskEnvelopeV1.** Build the envelope with jobId, inputHash, policyHash, budget, expiry, and nonce. Hash the canonical envelope to get the task hash. This task hash is your job identity. Share it in logs, in the dashboard, and in your receipt.

**Step 5 — Run Policy Check 1.** The Coordinator checks policy before any work. If the job violates budget, allowlist, quota, or expiry, it is rejected before assignment. This saves device time and money. Log the decision with policy version and reason.

**Step 6 — Assign and execute.** The Coordinator assigns a worker. EdgeAgent executes under CPU, memory, time, and battery limits. The worker signs the result. The signature binds job, assignment, digests, nonce, and policy. If the device goes offline, the job can be retried safely because the nonce and assignment make retries idempotent.

**Step 7 — Verify independently.** ProofAgent fetches the same pinned inputs, replays deterministic work, and compares canonical output bytes. It checks schema at E0, signature at E1, replay at E2, and corroboration at E3 when needed. It never trusts worker assertions. It writes a verification verdict with evidence level and rejection code if needed.

**Step 8 — Run Policy Check 2 and Exact Message Review.** After VERIFIED, Policy Check 2 re-validates budget and policy. Then the user sees the exact message to be signed: recipient, amount, memo, and job binding. The main wallet never auto-signs. Only the capped agent wallet signs, and only after human review in the demo flow.

**Step 9 — Settle on Solana.** The Coordinator builds a Solana Devnet USDC transaction, submits it, confirms it, and reconciles the reservation. Fees are about $0.0002 and settle is about 0.9 seconds in the demo. Record the transaction signature.

**Step 10 — Issue and check the receipt.** EdgeProof issues a signed receipt with task hash, result hash, worker DID, verifier DID, policy hash, and tx signature. Verify the receipt offline: check hashes, check signatures, check policy hash. Save the receipt. It is your portable proof.

const envelope = {
  jobId: "job_100_tutorial:_su",
  inputHash: "sha256:…", // hash of pinned inputs

  nonce: crypto.randomUUID(),

const taskHash = await hashCanonical(envelope);
// Policy Check 1
const admitted = await policyCheck1(envelope);
if (!admitted) throw new Error("Policy Check 1 rejected");
// Execute on EdgeAgent, sign with Ed25519
const result = await edgeAgent.execute(envelope);
// Verify with ProofAgent — never trust worker claim
const verdict = await proofAgent.verify(envelope, result);
if (verdict.status !== "VERIFIED") throw new Error(verdict.code);
// Policy Check 2 + Exact Message Review
await policyCheck2(envelope, verdict);
const tx = await buildSolanaPayment(envelope, verdict);
console.log("tx", tx.signature);
```pseudocode-unvalidated

The transaction is built only after verification. If any step fails, the job stops and the reservation is released. Notice what is missing: there is no step where the main wallet auto-signs, no step where a WARNING job pays, and no step where the Coordinator trusts the worker. Those omissions are the design. When you review code, check for those omissions. If you see a path where payment happens without VERIFIED, that is a bug. Fix it before mainnet.

## Best Practices for Tutorial: Submit to Solana Hackathon on MLH

**1. Keep jobs small and deterministic.** Small jobs verify faster and replay cleanly. If your job is nondeterministic, declare it. Do not pretend a random model output is deterministic. Use E3 corroboration for nondeterministic work, and label it honestly.

**2. Pin everything.** Pin inputs, models, code version, and policy. If it is not pinned, it cannot be verified. If it cannot be verified, it cannot be paid. Pinning is not bureaucracy. It is the only way the verifier can do its job.

**3. Use integer micro-USDC everywhere.** Never use floats for money. $0.10 is 100000 micro-USDC. Store it as an integer, reserve it atomically, and reconcile it to the on-chain amount. Floats cause rounding bugs that are hard to debug and easy to exploit.

**4. Log decisions with hashes.** Log task hash, result hash, policy hash, verifier DID, and verdict for every job. Logs without hashes are stories. Logs with hashes are evidence. You will need them for audit, for debugging, and for your hackathon demo.

**5. Test the failure path.** Test tampered results, expired jobs, over-budget jobs, offline workers, and failed verifications. The happy path is easy. The failure path is where trust is built. Write a test for each rejection code and show it in your demo.

## Common Pitfalls and Troubleshooting

**Pitfall: Hash mismatch after a tiny edit.** You changed one character in the input and verification failed. That is correct behavior. The hash changed. Re-pin the input, create a new envelope, and re-run. Do not try to patch the old hash.

**Pitfall: Policy Check 1 passes but Check 2 fails.** Policy changed between creation and verification, or budget was already spent by a concurrent job. Check policy version, check reservations, and re-create with fresh policy hash.

**Pitfall: Verifier says WARNING.** WARNING is not VERIFIED. WARNING never pays. Read the warning code, fix the input or the verifier, and re-run. Do not force a WARNING job to pay.

**Pitfall: Payment stuck or not confirmed.** Check the transaction signature on Devnet explorer, check reservation status, and check if the reservation expired. If it expired, the reservation is released and you need a new job. Do not retry the same transaction with a new nonce without checking reconciliation.

**Pitfall: Agent wallet shows $0 balance.** The agent wallet is intentionally small. Fund it with a small amount, like $2.50 USDC in the demo, and check caps. If it is empty, top it up from your main wallet with human approval and exact message review. Never auto-fund from main wallet.

## Security Notes for Tutorial: Submit to Solana Hackathon on MLH

Security for tutorial: submit to solana hackathon on mlh starts with separation. The main wallet never auto-signs. The agent wallet is capped. The worker and verifier are in separate trust boundaries. Signatures are domain-separated. Nonces and expiry prevent replay. Policy is versioned and hashed. If any of those separations break, stop and fix it. Do not ship a demo where the main wallet signs automatically, even if it is more convenient. Convenience is not worth a drained wallet. For tutorials, also think about privacy. Content never leaves the device unless the job requires it. Only hashes are anchored. If your job handles sensitive data, run it locally, pin the source, and verify the digest, not the raw content. Document what leaves the device and what stays. Judges and users will ask. Have an answer ready that matches your code.
